title: Money in One Level
objective: After this level you can explain the three jobs money does: a way to pay, a measure of value and a way to save.
summary: Money is anything that does three jobs: a medium of exchange, a unit of account and a store of value. In a WWII prison camp, cigarettes did all three.

cards.headline: In a WWII prison camp, cigarettes became money. Even non-smokers wanted them.
cards.body: Economist R. A. Radford was a prisoner there, and in 1945 he explained why. Cigarettes were doing the three jobs that make something money. Learn those three jobs and you know what money is.

cards.headline: Job 1: a way to pay
cards.body: Trade in the camp began as barter: my jam for your biscuits, if we each wanted what the other had. Then cigarettes took over. Everyone, non-smokers included, would sell for cigarettes, because they could spend them later on something else. That's a medium of exchange: something you accept not to use, but to pass on.

cards.headline: Job 2: a measure of value
cards.body: Soon every price in camp was quoted in cigarettes. Prisoners called out offers like "cheese for seven", and laundry cost two cigarettes a garment. Nobody had to work out what cheese was worth in jam. One common unit let anyone compare anything. That's a unit of account, the ruler you measure value with. Yours is probably dollars, euros or pounds.

mascot.line: Now you have all three jobs: a way to pay, a measure of value, a way to save. The whole tree builds on them.

cards.fact: Money you can smoke is a risky way to save.
cards.context: Job 3 is store of value: money should keep until you're ready to spend it. Prisoners did save cigarettes in reserve. The flaw? People also smoked them. When deliveries stopped, stocks ran out and prices fell. The camp's savings had literally gone up in smoke.

title: Before Money: Barter
objective: After this level you can explain how barter works and why it gets awkward.
summary: Barter means swapping goods directly. It needs a double coincidence of wants, has no common measure of value and makes saving hard. No pure barter economy has ever been described.

cards.headline: You fix cars. You want lunch. You need a farmer with a broken car.
cards.body: No money allowed. Before you can eat, you have to find someone who has food and also needs a mechanic today. Welcome to barter.

cards.headline: The lucky match barter needs
cards.body: Barter means trading one good or service directly for another, no money involved: your repair for their vegetables. It only works when each of you wants what the other has. Economists call that a double coincidence of wants, and it's rarer than it sounds. The farmer with the broken car does exist. Finding him before lunch is another matter.

cards.headline: No ruler, no savings
cards.body: Remember Level 1's three jobs? Barter struggles with them. There's no common ruler: without an agreed measure, every swap sets its own terms, and each deal stands on its own. Saving is hard too. Picture a farmer hoping to buy a tractor in six months with strawberries picked today. By then, they're jam at best.

mascot.line: The popular story says barter came first. Nobody has found a society that ran on barter alone.

cards.fact: Nobody has ever described a society that ran on barter alone.
cards.context: The textbook story, going back to Adam Smith, says people bartered first and switched to money once they saw it worked better. In 1985, anthropologist Caroline Humphrey concluded that no pure barter economy has ever been described. Barter is real, though. It tends to happen between people who know each other, or when money runs short: in Level 1's camp, whenever cigarette deliveries stopped, trade slid back toward barter.

title: Shells, Salt and Stones
objective: After this level you can describe early forms of money like cowrie shells and explain why they worked.
summary: Cowrie shells, salt bars and Yap's giant stones all worked as money. Shells were small, durable and hard to fake; Yap's stones changed owners without moving.

cards.headline: Money has been shells, salt and stone wheels wider than a car.
cards.body: None of it was silly. Each one did Level 1's jobs well enough that people trusted it. Here's what made three very different moneys work.

cards.headline: Cowries: money from the sea
cards.body: Cowrie shells were small, light, durable and hard to fake: most of a money wish list. They served as money in parts of Africa, in places until the late 1800s. In China, strings of cowries were used as payments from around 1000 BCE, and the link stuck. Many Chinese characters about money, like those for buy, loan and tax, still contain the ancient symbol for a shell.
cards.callout: 貝 (bei): shell · 買 buy · 貸 loan · 賦 tax

cards.fact: In Ethiopia, bars of salt were money for centuries.
cards.context: They stayed in use right up to the 1930s. Salt had a big advantage: nearly everyone needs it, so nearly everyone would take it. Like Level 1's cigarettes, it was worth something even to people who weren't planning to spend it.

cards.headline: Yap: money too big to move
cards.body: On the Pacific island of Yap, money came as stone discs quarried on Palau, hundreds of kilometers away across the sea. The biggest are more than 3.5 meters across, so they rarely went anywhere. When one changed hands, it stayed put, and everyone simply knew who the new owner was. In one story, a stone sank in a storm on the way home. The islanders agreed it still counted.

title: The First Coins
objective: After this level you can explain where the first coins came from and why metal made good money.
summary: The first coins were probably made in Lydia, in modern Turkey, around 650 BCE: electrum lumps of standard weight, stamped so no one had to weigh them.

cards.headline: The first coins probably came from a kingdom you've never heard of.
cards.body: Lydia, in what's now Turkey, around 650 BCE. And the big idea wasn't the metal. People had paid with metal for ages. It was the little picture pressed into it.

cards.headline: The trouble with lumps
cards.body: Before coins, traders paid with rings and bars of gold and silver. Metal made fine money: it's portable, it doesn't rot like Level 2's strawberries, and it's hard to fake. The catch? Every deal meant weighing the metal and checking it. Imagine a set of scales at every checkout.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing here: the stamp was the invention, not the metal.

cards.headline: A stamp you could trust
cards.body: Lydia's coins were lumps of electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver, made to strict standard weights. Many carried a lion's head, which seems to have been a royal symbol. The stamp marked the coin as official money that the state would accept as payment. No scales, no testing: you just counted. That's the whole trick of a coin.

cards.fact: As rich as Croesus? He's often credited with the first pure gold and silver coins.
cards.context: Electrum mixed metals, so its worth was hard to pin down. Lydia fixed that by minting separate gold and silver coins, often credited to the legendarily wealthy King Croesus, though some were probably made before and after his reign. The idea spread fast around the Mediterranean. Meanwhile, China had its own coins, probably invented independently: bronze, cast in the shapes of spades and knives.

title: Paper Money
objective: After this level you can explain how paper money began in China and spread around the world.
summary: Paper money began in China: Tang merchants' flying money, then Song-era notes in Sichuan, where iron coins were heavy. Europe's first banknotes came from Sweden in 1661.

cards.headline: Paper money was invented because coins were too heavy. Literally.
cards.body: In 11th-century China, and again in 17th-century Sweden, people's coins were so heavy that a paper promise was simply easier to carry.

cards.headline: Flying money
cards.body: It started with merchants in Tang dynasty China (618–907). Rather than haul heavy coins on long journeys, they used paper drafts nicknamed "flying money". Was that the first paper money? The British Museum says yes; other historians call it a draft for moving funds, more like a money order than cash. Either way, paper had started standing in for metal.

cards.headline: Sichuan's iron problem
cards.body: In 11th-century Sichuan, people used iron coins, which were heavy. So they left their coins on deposit and carried paper certificates instead, which could be spent in their place. Around 1023, the Song government took over issuing them. These notes, called jiaozi, are widely described as the world's first paper currency.

cards.fact: Europe's first real banknotes came from Sweden in 1661.
cards.context: Marco Polo had described China's paper money back in the 13th century. Then Stockholms Banco issued notes, and they caught on for a familiar reason: Sweden's copper coins were heavy and cumbersome. But paper is only a promise. When the public lost confidence in the bank, it failed. Why people trust paper at all is Level 6's question.

title: Why Money Has Value
objective: After this level you can explain why money is valuable because people trust it and accept it.
summary: Today's money is fiat money: legal tender backed by no commodity. A $100 bill costs about 11 cents to print; its value comes from trust that others will accept it.

cards.headline: A $100 bill costs about 11 cents to print. So why is it worth $100?
cards.body: Paper, ink and labor came to about 11 cents a note in the Federal Reserve's 2025 figures. Everything else comes from something you can't see or touch.

cards.headline: Fiat money
cards.body: Look at a US bill. It says: "This note is legal tender for all debts, public and private." Nothing about gold, or anything else behind it. That's fiat money: it has no value of its own, and a government declares it legal tender. Today's dollars are fiat money. Their only backing, as one economics textbook puts it, is shared faith and trust that they have value.

mascot.line: Keep this one: money works because everyone expects everyone else to accept it.

cards.headline: A chain of confidence
cards.body: Picture the chain. A baker takes your bill because her flour supplier will take it from her, and he takes it because his landlord will. Everyone accepts it because everyone else does. It's the logic of Level 1's camp, where non-smokers took cigarettes because others would take them later. Money works because people believe it will.

cards.fact: A stone on the seabed can be money. It all comes down to belief.
cards.context: Remember Level 3's sunken stone on Yap? In 1991, economist Milton Friedman used it to show how much money rests on unquestioned belief, and he meant our money too. The flip side follows. When belief goes, paper is just paper, as Level 5's Swedish bank found out when the public lost confidence.

title: The Gold Standard
objective: After this level you can explain what the gold standard was and why countries left it.
summary: Under a gold standard, money is tied to a fixed amount of gold. Gold's supply couldn't keep pace with growing economies, and the dollar's last gold link ended in 1971.

cards.headline: For generations, a paper note was a ticket you could cash in for gold.
cards.body: Hand over your notes, walk away with metal. Then, country by country, the deal ended. The last big link snapped on August 15, 1971.

cards.headline: Money tied to metal
cards.body: Under a gold standard, a country's unit of money is a fixed amount of gold. Britain adopted one in 1821, and by the 1870s other big economies, including Germany and France, had followed. In the US, the Federal Reserve had to swap dollars for gold at a fixed price. The appeal was simple: paper you could trust, because gold stood behind it.

cards.headline: The golden handcuffs
cards.body: The catch: the supply of newly mined gold has nothing to do with how much money a growing economy needs. In hard times, that tied governments' hands. World War I pushed countries off gold, the Great Depression finished the job, and by 1937 no country kept a full gold standard. In 1933, the US stopped swapping money for gold coins and bars at home.

cards.fact: In 1971, Nixon "temporarily" cut the dollar's last link to gold.
cards.context: After World War II, the Bretton Woods system fixed other currencies to the dollar, and dollars to gold at $35 an ounce. Foreign governments could still cash their dollars in. On August 15, 1971, President Nixon said he had told the Treasury to "suspend temporarily" that swap. The system soon ended, and the world's money became fiat money: Level 6's kind, backed by trust.

title: Money as Numbers
objective: After this level you can explain why most money today exists only as numbers in bank records.
summary: Most money today is bank deposits, records of what banks owe you. In the UK, 97% of money is deposits. Paying by card just changes two balances.

cards.headline: Most of your money has never been printed.
cards.body: In the UK, 97% of the money people hold isn't notes or coins at all. It's numbers in banks' records. (That's the Bank of England's figure from 2014.)

mascot.line: Keep this: your balance is a record of what the bank owes you. Levels 9 and 22 build on it.

cards.headline: Your balance is a promise
cards.body: A bank deposit isn't a pile of your cash in a vault. It's a record of what the bank owes you, a kind of IOU. Money today is a special IOU, one that everyone in the economy trusts. That's why most people get paid in deposits, and many never swap them back into cash.

cards.headline: Paying without anything moving
cards.body: Pay for a coffee by debit card and no cash travels anywhere. The banks just edit two numbers: your balance goes down and the café's goes up. The payment is the change to the record. You used your deposit as money without ever touching a coin.

cards.fact: Yap's islanders would find your bank account oddly familiar.
cards.context: On Level 3's Yap, a stone could change owners without moving. In the early 1930s, the New York Fed did much the same with gold: rather than ship it across the ocean to the Bank of France, it moved bars into drawers in its own vault labeled as French. Milton Friedman, who told both stories, pointed out that most of our wealth, bank balances included, is something we never actually see.

title: Cryptocurrency
objective: After this level you can explain what cryptocurrencies are and how they differ from money in a bank.
summary: Cryptocurrencies like bitcoin are digital tokens recorded on a blockchain, a shared ledger kept by a network. With a nearly fixed supply, bitcoin's price swings sharply.

cards.headline: Bitcoin has no bank, no boss and no building. So who keeps the books?
cards.body: Level 8's money lives in a bank's records. Bitcoin's records are kept by a whole network of computers at once, with no bank, company or government in charge.

cards.headline: Money without a middleman
cards.body: In October 2008, someone calling themselves Satoshi Nakamoto proposed bitcoin: a digital currency that wouldn't rely on banks or governments. It launched in 2009, and nobody knows for sure who Nakamoto is. Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, named for its heavy use of cryptography, the mathematics of codes. There are no bitcoin coins or notes. It exists only as entries in its own records.

cards.headline: A ledger everyone holds
cards.body: Those records form a blockchain: a ledger of transactions shared across the network. Transactions are bundled into blocks, and each block carries a cryptographic fingerprint of the one before. Change an old entry and every later link breaks, so tampering is easy to spot. To spend, you sign with a secret private key. Lose it and the coins are gone for good. Researchers have compared all this to Level 3's Yap, whose islanders kept a shared record of who owned each stone.

cards.fact: Bitcoin's price can skyrocket or tumble within days.
cards.context: Its price is set by supply and demand, and the supply is capped at just under 21 million coins. With supply more or less fixed, every swing in demand lands on the price: a cousin of Level 7's gold problem. Supporters see that fixed supply as a hedge against inflation. Critics, including the European Central Bank, say the swings make it too unstable to be Level 1's store of value.

cards.headline: The six-trait test

title: Where Income Comes From
objective: After this level you can explain the main ways people earn money: wages, profits, interest and rent.
summary: Economists group what it takes to make things into land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship. Each earns its own income: rent, wages, interest and profit. Wages are most people's main income.

cards.headline: One slice of pizza pays four different kinds of income.
cards.body: The cook, the landlord, the lender behind the oven and the owner of the shop all get a cut of what you paid. Economists have a name for each cut. Learn the four and you'll start seeing them everywhere.

cards.headline: Four ingredients for making anything
cards.body: Making anything, from pizza to phones, takes four ingredients. Economists call them the factors of production. Land is any natural resource, like water, oil or forests. Labor is people's work. Capital is the tools, machinery and buildings, like hammers, computers and delivery vans. Entrepreneurship is the person who combines the other three to earn a profit. So when an economist says capital, picture the oven, not the cash.

mascot.line: Keep this: profit is whatever is left after wages, rent and interest are paid.

cards.headline: Every ingredient gets paid
cards.body: Each factor earns its own kind of income. Land earns rent. Labor earns wages. Capital earns interest. Entrepreneurship earns profit, and profit is whatever is left after the wages, rent and interest have been paid. In the pizza shop, the owner gets paid last.

Wages go to anyone who sells their work, and they're the largest source of income for most people. Remember Level 8? Most people now receive that pay as bank deposits, and many never swap it back into cash.

title: Gross and Net Pay
objective: After this level you can explain why take-home pay is smaller than the salary on a job offer.
summary: Gross pay is what you earn; net pay is what arrives after withholding. In the US, payroll taxes take 7.65% before income tax and other deductions.

cards.headline: The salary on your job offer never lands in your bank account.
cards.body: Not all of it, anyway. Before your pay reaches you, your employer takes some out and sends it elsewhere. Your first paycheck is where you find out how much.

mascot.line: People mix these up all the time. Gross is the whole pizza; net is the slices that reach your plate.

cards.headline: Gross comes first, net comes home
cards.body: Your gross pay is everything you earn from your wages or salary, before anything is taken out. Your net pay, also called take-home pay, is what you actually receive after tax withholding and other deductions. Gross is what you earn. Net is what you get.

cards.headline: Who gets a slice first
cards.body: Your employer withholds part of every paycheck to cover payroll taxes and income tax, and sends it to the government. In the US, the payroll taxes are called FICA: Social Security and Medicare. Federal income tax rates are the same nationwide, and some states and localities add their own. Money can also come out for retirement savings or health insurance. Your pay passes several tollbooths on the way to you.

cards.fact: On a $1,000 paycheck, $76.50 goes to payroll taxes alone.
cards.context: That's 6.2% for Social Security plus 1.45% for Medicare, 7.65% in all: $62.00 and $14.50. Your employer also pays its own matching share on top, which never appears in your pay at all. Income tax, and any retirement or health deductions, come out as well.

title: Budgets
objective: After this level you can build a simple budget that separates needs, wants and saving.
summary: A budget is a written monthly plan: list expenses, note income, subtract. The popular 50/30/20 rule splits after-tax income into needs, wants and saving.

cards.headline: Your budget is named after a leather bag.
cards.body: The word comes from the Old French bougette, a small leather bag. Its money meaning dates from 1733, from the picture of a treasury minister keeping his financial plans in one. Yours can live in a notebook or an app. The job hasn't changed.

cards.headline: A plan you write down
cards.body: A budget is a plan you write down to decide how you'll spend your money each month. Making one takes three steps: list your bills and other expenses, write down your monthly income, then subtract. The answer should be more than zero. If it's below zero, you're spending more than you make, and something in the plan has to change. Arithmetic is not moved by optimism.

cards.headline: Three buckets: 50, 30, 20
cards.body: One popular way to split the money was popularized by Elizabeth Warren and her daughter Amelia Warren Tyagi in their book All Your Worth. Put 50% of after-tax income toward needs, 30% toward wants and 20% toward saving or paying down debt. After-tax is Level 12's net pay: the buckets are filled from what actually arrives.

cards.fact: The 50/30/20 rule is a guideline, not a law of physics.
cards.context: It's meant to get you thinking about where each paycheck goes, not to be followed to the dollar. Whatever split you use, a budget runs as a monthly loop: make the plan at the start, write down what you spend each day, and check at the end of the month whether you spent what you planned.

title: Needs and Wants
objective: After this level you can tell needs from wants and explain why the line differs from person to person.
summary: Needs are essential to survival and basic living; wants are for enjoyment. Adam Smith showed that custom moves the line: a linen shirt or leather shoes could be a need in one place and not another.

cards.headline: Is a linen shirt a need? In 1776, it depended where you lived.
cards.body: Adam Smith took the question seriously in The Wealth of Nations. His answer explains why your list of needs won't match everybody else's.

cards.headline: Needs keep you going. Wants make it nicer.
cards.body: Needs are the things essential to survival and basic living: food, shelter, clothing, utilities. Wants are the things you'd like for enjoyment or lifestyle. Level 13's 50/30/20 rule gives them separate buckets. The tricky part is that a need can come in a want-sized version. You need food. Dining out every night is a want.

cards.headline: Smith's shirt test
cards.body: Smith defined necessaries as more than what keeps you alive. They also included whatever local custom made it shameful for respectable people to go without. A linen shirt isn't strictly needed for life: the ancient Greeks and Romans lived comfortably without linen. Yet a respectable day-labourer of Smith's time would be ashamed to appear in public without one. Same shirt, different century, different category.

cards.fact: In Smith's day, leather shoes were a need in England, half a need in Scotland and no need in France.
cards.context: Custom made them a necessity for both men and women in England, for men but not women in Scotland, and for neither in France, where people could go in wooden shoes or barefoot without shame. The line between needs and wants isn't drawn by nature. Where you live, and when, helps draw it.

title: Opportunity Cost
objective: After this level you can explain that every choice costs the next best thing you give up.
summary: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative you give up. College costs lost earnings as well as tuition, and time always counts: there's no such thing as a free lunch.

cards.headline: American saloons once gave away lunch. There was a catch.
cards.body: In the 1800s and early 1900s, the free lunch came with a condition: you had to buy a drink. The sign said free; the bar tab said otherwise. Economists later turned the joke into a rule.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this level: every choice costs the next best thing you gave up.

cards.headline: The price tag you don't see
cards.body: Every choice has a cost that never shows up on a receipt. Economists call it opportunity cost: the value of the next best alternative, the thing you gave up by choosing. Sleep through a class and the cost isn't money. It's the learning you missed. Pick pizza for dinner and the cost is the burger you didn't have.

cards.headline: College's hidden bill
cards.body: College has out-of-pocket costs: tuition, books and the rest. It also has an opportunity cost. While you're in class or studying, you can't be working at a paying job, so the earnings you give up are part of the price. For college, that opportunity cost is bigger than the money cost. The largest part of the bill never arrives in the mail.

cards.fact: Time is part of the price of everything.
cards.context: Spend 3 hours and $20 at the movies the night before an exam, and the cost isn't just the $20. It's also the study time you gave up. So even when a lunch is free, the hour you spend on it isn't. That's the saloon lesson: there's no such thing as a free lunch. The saying was an economic maxim by 1938, and Milton Friedman used a version of it as a book title in 1975.

title: How Prices Nudge You
objective: After this level you can spot common pricing tricks like prices ending in 99 and decoy options.
summary: Most shoppers don't know what a price should be, so cues steer them: a dress sold better at $39 than $34, and the word "sale" lifted demand. A decoy option can make its neighbor look like a bargain.

cards.headline: A dress sold better at $39 than at $34.
cards.body: In a catalog study by Eric Anderson and Duncan Simester, raising the price lifted demand by about a third. Higher price, more buyers. Something other than the number was doing the selling.

cards.headline: Why the 9 works
cards.body: For most things you buy, you don't really know what the price should be. Nobody carries the fair price of a dress around in their head. So shoppers lean on cues, signals that hint at a bargain, and a price ending in 9 is one of them. In the dress study, that little 9 did better than an actual $5 discount.

cards.headline: The word that sells
cards.body: Another cue is a single word. In catalog tests, putting "sale" beside a price increased demand by more than 50%. It works for the same reason as the 9: you can't easily check the price yourself, so the sign does the judging for you.

cards.headline: The option nobody buys
cards.body: Picture a coffee shop with a small for $3 and a large for $5. Now it adds a medium priced just under the large. Hardly anyone orders the medium, but suddenly the large looks like a steal. That's the decoy effect: adding a third, less attractive option changes how people choose between the original two. The decoy's job isn't to sell. It's to make its neighbor look brilliant.

title: Paying by Card
objective: After this level you can explain how a card payment works and who pays the fees.
summary: A card payment runs from the merchant's bank through the card network to your bank and back. The merchant pays a fee, mostly interchange to your bank, and passes it on in prices, even to cash users.

cards.headline: One tap for a coffee puts four parties to work.
cards.body: You, the café, your bank and the café's bank all play a part. One of them pays a fee for the privilege. It isn't you. At least, not directly.

cards.headline: Ask, approve, pay
cards.body: When you tap, the café's bank (the acquirer) sends a request through the card network, like Visa or Mastercard, to the bank that issued your card. Your bank checks that the account is valid and approves. Then the acquirer settles the sale, paying the café with money from your bank. Remember Level 8? Nothing physical travels. Balances change.

cards.headline: The café pays to get paid
cards.body: Card payments aren't free for the seller. The café pays a merchant discount fee on each sale, and most of it goes to your bank as an interchange fee. The card networks set that fee; for credit cards it generally runs from about 1 to 3 percent of the price. So the café receives a little less than the price on the menu.
cards.callout: Interchange: set by the network, paid to your bank

cards.fact: Pay with cash and you may still be paying card fees.
cards.context: Shops generally cover card costs through higher prices for everyone, because they usually charge card and cash customers the same. A 2010 Boston Fed study concluded that cash users in effect pay part of the cost of card fees and rewards. The fee isn't on your receipt. It's folded into the price.

title: Small Costs Add Up

title: Scams and Fraud
objective: After this level you can recognize common money scams and their warning signs.
summary: The FTC's four signs of a scam: pretend, problem or prize, pressure, and pay in a specific way. People reported losing more than $12.5 billion to fraud in 2024.

cards.headline: The caller says he's from the government. He wants payment in gift cards.
cards.body: That's all you need to know. No real business or government agency will ever tell you to buy a gift card to pay them.

cards.headline: Pretend, then a problem or a prize
cards.body: Scams come in endless costumes, but the FTC boils them down to four signs. First, scammers pretend to be from an organization you know: the government, a utility, a tech company. Second, they say there's a problem (you owe money, your account needs verifying) or a prize you've won. The costume changes. The script doesn't.

mascot.line: Keep the checklist: pretend, problem or prize, pressure, pay. Hear all four, and hang up.

cards.headline: Then hurry, and pay this way
cards.body: Third, they pressure you to act immediately, before you have time to think, sometimes with threats of arrest or a lawsuit. Fourth, they tell you exactly how to pay: cryptocurrency, a money wire, a payment app or a gift card. A real problem can wait while you hang up and check. A scam can't.

cards.fact: In 2024, people told the FTC they lost more than $12.5 billion to fraud.
cards.context: Impostors, people pretending to be someone they're not, were the most commonly reported scam. And people lost more through payments by bank transfer or cryptocurrency than through all other payment methods combined. Those are exactly the ways of paying that sign four warns about.

cards.headline: Engel's discovery

Economists call it Engel's law. Food is Level 14's classic need, and Engel showed how much room it takes up at different incomes.

title: What Banks Do
objective: After this level you can explain how banks take deposits and make loans.
summary: Banks grew out of medieval money changers' benches. A bank takes deposits and makes loans, standing between savers and borrowers, and earns on the spread between the two interest rates.

cards.headline: Why is it called a bank? Blame a wooden bench.
cards.body: In medieval Italy, money changers did business at a banco, a bench or table. Along the way they invented the job every bank still does.

cards.headline: Deposits in, loans out
cards.body: Lombard money changers started out swapping coins for foreign merchants and travelers. Then clients began leaving money with them for safekeeping, and anyone who wanted to borrow could come to the changer, who lent those deposits out. That's still the heart of banking: a bank accepts deposits and makes loans.

cards.headline: The middleman
cards.body: Economists call a bank a financial intermediary. It sits between savers who deposit money and borrowers who take out loans. Without one, a saver with spare cash would have to hunt down someone who wanted to borrow it and trust them to pay it back. Remember barter's lucky match from Level 2? A bank spares savers and borrowers from having to find each other.

mascot.line: Keep this: a bank borrows at one rate and lends at a higher one. The spread is its living.

cards.fact: A bank earns its living in the gap between two interest rates.
cards.context: It pays interest on deposits and charges a higher rate on its loans. The difference is called the spread, and it covers the bank's costs and its profit. The benches got fancier over the centuries. The business model barely changed.

title: How Banks Create Money
objective: After this level you can explain how bank lending creates most of the money in circulation.
summary: A new bank loan creates a matching deposit: new money. Most money today starts this way. Repaying destroys it, and profit, risk, rules and interest rates limit it.

cards.headline: When a bank lends you money, it doesn't hand you anyone's savings.
cards.body: It creates a brand-new deposit in your account. According to the Bank of England, that's where most of today's money comes from.

cards.headline: Money at the stroke of a pen
cards.body: Say you take out a mortgage to buy a house. The bank doesn't count out banknotes. It credits your account with a new deposit the size of the loan, and at that moment new money exists that didn't before. Some economists call this "fountain pen money", created at the stroke of a banker's pen when a loan is approved. The pen is optional these days.

mascot.line: Easy to get backwards: banks don't lend out deposits first. The loan creates the deposit.

cards.headline: Level 21, flipped
cards.body: Level 21 showed a bank standing between savers and borrowers. The Bank of England says the order usually runs the other way: rather than lending out deposits that savers placed with them, banks create deposits by lending. That's how Level 8's 97% came about. Most of the money people hold in banks started life as somebody's loan.

cards.fact: Paying off a loan makes money disappear.
cards.context: Repaying a bank loan destroys the deposit that lending created. And banks can't create money without limit: they must lend profitably and manage their risks, regulators set rules, and the central bank's interest rates act as the ultimate brake.

title: Interest

summary: Interest is the price of borrowing, usually a yearly rate. Lenders charge for waiting and for risk. Hammurabi's laws set interest rates over 1,000 years before coins.

cards.headline: Interest is older than coins.
cards.body: Mesopotamian laws, including Hammurabi's code, were setting interest rates in the 18th century BCE. Lydia's first coins from Level 4 came more than 1,000 years later, around 650 BCE. People have been paying to borrow for a very long time.

cards.headline: Rent for money
cards.body: Interest is the price of borrowing: the fee a borrower pays a lender for the use of money. It's usually quoted as a rate. Borrow $100 at 5% a year, and a year's use of that money costs you $5. Think of it as rent. You get to use someone else's money for a while, and like a rented flat, it goes back at the end, with the rent on top.

cards.headline: Why lenders charge
cards.body: Lending means waiting. If someone would pay $95 today for a promise of $100 in a year, the $5 difference is interest, the reward for giving up money now. Risk raises the price too. Mesopotamian law allowed 20% on loans of silver but more on barley, because barley loans usually went to the poor and were seen as riskier.

cards.fact: Interest runs both ways.
cards.context: When you borrow, you pay it. When you deposit money in certain accounts, the bank may pay you. Level 21's spread lives in the gap between those two rates: the bank charges borrowers more than it pays savers.

title: Compound Interest
objective: After this level you can explain how earning interest on interest makes money grow faster over time.
summary: Compound interest pays interest on earlier interest, so growth speeds up. Franklin calculated £1,000 at 5% would become £131,000 in a century, not £6,000. The Rule of 72 estimates doubling time.

cards.headline: Ben Franklin left Boston £1,000 and a 200-year homework assignment.
cards.body: In his will, he asked for the money to be lent out at interest to young tradesmen, and he did the math on what would happen. His answer shows why interest on interest is such a big deal.

mascot.line: Hold on to the snowball. Level 25 shows it rolling the other way, on debts.

cards.headline: Interest on interest
cards.body: Simple interest is paid only on the amount you started with. Compound interest is paid on that amount plus all the interest it has already earned. So each year's interest joins the pile that earns next year's. The pile grows, so the interest grows, so the pile grows faster. It's a snowball rolling downhill, picking up snow that picks up more snow.

cards.fact: £1,000 at 5% for 100 years: Franklin reckoned it would become £131,000.
cards.context: With simple interest, £50 a year for 100 years adds just £5,000, for £6,000 in all. Compounding made a difference of about £125,000. Reality was messier: the funds were badly managed and fell short of his estimates. Even so, by 1990 Boston's fund had grown to about $4.5 million.

cards.headline: The Rule of 72
cards.body: Here's a shortcut for compounding: divide 72 by the yearly interest rate to estimate how many years it takes money to double. At 8%, about 9 years. At 2%, about 36. The rate matters enormously: quadruple the rate from 2% to 8% and the money doubles four times as fast.

title: Credit Cards and Debt
objective: After this level you can explain how credit card interest can turn a small debt into a big one.
summary: A credit card is revolving credit. Paying in full may avoid interest; unpaid balances compound at high rates. US statements must warn about paying only the minimum.

cards.headline: Every US credit card bill carries a warning label.
cards.body: Not about your health. Federal rules require it on every statement, and it's about one choice: paying only the minimum.

cards.headline: A loan every time you tap
cards.body: A credit card is revolving credit: you can borrow up to a set limit, then repay in one go or bit by bit. Pay the whole balance by the due date, and you may not be charged interest on purchases at all. Leave part unpaid, and that part is charged interest. It's the same card either way. What changes is whether it's working as a way to pay or as a loan.

cards.headline: The snowball, in reverse
cards.body: Level 24's snowball works on debts too. Unpaid interest is added to the balance, and then interest is charged on the lot. That's how card debt can balloon. And card rates are steep: in 2026, US card accounts charged interest paid about 22% a year on average. By the Rule of 72, a balance growing at 22% would double in a little over three years if nothing were paid.

cards.fact: The warning: pay only the minimum, and you pay more interest for longer.
cards.context: The statement must also estimate how long paying only the minimum would take to clear the balance, and what it would cost in total. It's Level 24's math, printed with your own numbers.

title: Credit Scores
objective: After this level you can explain what a credit score measures and what raises or lowers it.
summary: A credit score predicts how likely you are to repay on time, from your credit reports. FICO weighs payment history most, then amounts owed. Income is not part of it, and there is no single score.

cards.headline: Lenders can size you up without ever meeting you.
cards.body: They look at a number built from your borrowing record. Most of these numbers fall between 300 and 850. What goes into one is less mysterious than it seems.

cards.headline: A forecast, not a grade
cards.body: A credit score is a prediction: how likely you are to pay back a loan on time, worked out from the record of your past borrowing in your credit reports. Usually a higher score makes a loan easier to get and may bring a better interest rate. Remember Level 23's barley loans: more risk, higher rate. A score is how a lender estimates the risk.

cards.headline: What's in the recipe
cards.body: FICO scores weigh five things. Paying on time is the biggest single slice, and how much you owe comes next. The length of your credit history, new credit and your mix of credit types fill in the rest. In other words, the score mostly watches what you do with borrowed money.

title: Mortgages
objective: After this level you can explain how a mortgage works and why it lasts for decades.
summary: A mortgage, a 'dead pledge', lets the lender take the property if it isn't repaid. Longer terms mean smaller payments but more total cost; early payments are mostly interest.

cards.headline: A mortgage is, word for word, a "dead pledge".
cards.body: The name comes from Old French. It's less grim than it sounds, and it explains exactly how a home loan works.

cards.headline: Why the pledge dies
cards.body: The pledge is the property. A mortgage gives the lender the right to take it if you don't repay the loan plus interest. So the pledge dies one of two ways: the debt is paid off and the lender's claim ends, or the payments stop and the borrower loses the home. Either way, the deal is over.

cards.headline: Why decades?
cards.body: Spreading a big loan over many years makes each payment smaller. Compared with a 15-year mortgage, a 30-year one usually has lower monthly payments, but a higher interest rate and a higher total cost. More years of borrowing means more years of paying Level 23's rent on the money.

cards.fact: Your first mortgage payments mostly pay interest.
cards.context: Early on, the balance is high, so most of each payment covers interest. As the balance shrinks, more goes to paying off the loan itself, until near the end most of it does. This is amortization, and it's why the share of the home you own grows much more slowly than the payments you've made.

cards.headline: Secured: backed by something

Because the lender has a fallback, secured loans are less risky for it, so they usually come with lower interest rates and higher borrowing limits.

cards.headline: Unsecured: backed by you

title: When Banks Fail
objective: After this level you can explain bank runs and how deposit insurance protects savers.
summary: Banks borrow short and lend long, so they can't pay everyone at once. A run feeds itself. US deposit insurance covers $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category.

cards.headline: In a single day in 2023, customers pulled more than $40 billion out of one bank.
cards.body: The bank was Silicon Valley Bank, and regulators seized it the next day. To see how that can happen, look at what a bank does with your deposit.

cards.headline: Why no bank can pay everyone at once
cards.body: You can withdraw a deposit any day, but a bank's loans run for years. Economists call this borrowing short and lending long maturity transformation. Banks keep funds in reserve for depositors who want their money, but they can't pay off all their depositors at once.

cards.headline: The rush that feeds itself
cards.body: A bank run is when many depositors try to withdraw at the same time, and it can put a bank out of business. Here's the trap: once a run starts, the bank really is at risk, so it makes sense for everyone else to withdraw too. Economists Douglas Diamond and Philip Dybvig worked out that logic, and it helped earn them the 2022 Nobel Prize in economics. It's Level 6 in reverse: money works because people believe it will, and a run is what happens when belief cracks.

cards.fact: Since 1933, no depositor has lost a penny of FDIC-insured money.
cards.context: The US answer to runs is deposit insurance. The FDIC was created in 1933, after thousands of bank failures, to keep public confidence in the banking system. Today it covers $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each ownership category.

title: Why Save?
objective: After this level you can explain emergency funds and saving for goals.
summary: An emergency fund is cash kept safe and reachable for unplanned bills; goal saving targets costs you can see coming. Safe, handy savings usually earn a low interest rate.

cards.headline: A surprise $400 bill lands today. Could you pay it without borrowing?
cards.body: Every year the US Federal Reserve asks adults that question. In its survey for 2024, 63% said they'd cover it with cash or its equivalent. Another 13% said they couldn't pay it by any means. The gap between those answers has a name: savings.

cards.headline: An emergency fund has one job: be there
cards.body: An emergency fund is cash set aside for the bills nobody plans: a car repair, a medical bill, a cracked phone, a lost paycheck. Because emergencies don't wait, it lives somewhere safe and easy to reach, like a bank account, and somewhere you won't be tempted to dip into. A fund you raid for concert tickets is just a wallet with ambitions.

cards.headline: Goal saving: the bills you can see coming
cards.body: Other saving has a target on it: a laptop, a trip, a bike. Here the trick is naming it. The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau points out that having a specific goal for your savings can help you stay motivated. "Money for the laptop" is harder to spend on snacks than "some money". Divide the price by the months you have, and a big number becomes a small monthly one.

mascot.line: Notice the trade-off: safe and handy usually means slow. Level 32 picks it up.

cards.headline: Safe, handy and a little sleepy
cards.body: Remember Level 1's prisoners? Their cigarette reserves were a store of value until people smoked them. Savings only work if they keep. So they usually sit in safe places you can reach any time, like savings accounts. The catch: that safety and access come at a price, a low interest rate. Money that's always ready to go rarely has time to grow.

title: Risk and Return
objective: After this level you can explain why higher possible returns come with higher risk.
summary: Risk is uncertainty about what an investment will return. From 1928 to 2025, US stocks grew far more than Treasury bills but had big losing years; investors want higher returns for taking more risk.

cards.headline: $100 in 1928: one path passed $1 million, the other about $2,600.
cards.body: Put $100 into big US companies' stocks at the start of 1928, reinvest the dividends, and by the end of 2025 you'd have had over $1 million, before inflation. The same $100 in short-term US government loans called Treasury bills: about $2,600. So why would anyone pick the bills?

cards.headline: Risk means not knowing
cards.body: In finance, risk is uncertainty: you don't know what your return will be, and you might lose money. Stocks were the uncertain path. Their worst year was 1931, when they lost more than 40%, and they lost money in 26 of the 98 years. Treasury bills never had a single losing year. Slow, yes. Scary, never.

cards.headline: Why risk gets paid
cards.body: Nobody takes the rollercoaster for the same fare as the bus. As investment risks rise, investors seek higher returns to make up for them. That's the risk-return tradeoff: the chance of a bigger reward comes packaged with the chance of loss. Time matters too. Someone with decades to wait can sit through bad years; someone who needs the money next month may not want the ride at all.

cards.fact: The past is a record, not a promise.
cards.context: The 1928 to 2025 numbers tell you what did happen. They can't tell you what will. As the US Securities and Exchange Commission puts it, past performance is real historical information, but it cannot predict future performance. Risk means exactly that: the years ahead might look different.

title: What a Stock Is
objective: After this level you can explain what owning a share of a company means.
summary: A share of stock is a slice of ownership in a company. Shareholders can gain from dividends and rising prices, but can also lose. In 1602 the VOC became the first company to sell shares to the public.

cards.headline: In 1602, a new Dutch company invited the public to buy a piece of it.
cards.body: The Dutch East India Company, the VOC, invited the public in, and 1,143 investors signed up in Amsterdam alone. It's considered the first publicly traded company. Those investors weren't lending it money. They were buying ownership, and that's still what a share of stock is.

cards.headline: A share is a slice of a company
cards.body: A stock (or share) gives you a slice of ownership in a company. Companies sell shares to raise money: to pay off debt, launch products or build new facilities. Owning common stock usually gets you a vote at shareholder meetings. Hold one share of a giant company and you really do own a sliver of it. Just don't try taking a desk home.

cards.headline: Two ways a share can pay
cards.body: Shareholders can gain in two ways. Dividends: the company hands out part of its earnings. Capital appreciation: the share rises in price and is worth more than you paid. Neither is promised. Stock prices move down as well as up, there's no guarantee the company will do well, and you can lose money.

cards.fact: The first dividend was paid in spice.
cards.context: The VOC paid nothing until 1610, then handed shareholders mace, a spice, worth 75% of the share capital. Selling up worked differently too: the company's bookkeeper recorded the new owner in a register. Like Level 3's Yap stones, ownership changed hands in the record.

title: What a Bond Is
objective: After this level you can explain how a bond works as a loan to a government or company.
summary: A bond is an IOU: you lend to an issuer that pays interest and returns the face value at maturity. Bondholders are paid before shareholders. Britain's War Loan ran from 1917 to 2015.

cards.headline: In 2015, Britain repaid money it borrowed in 1917 to fight World War I.
cards.body: By then more than 120,000 holders were still owed a share of it, and still collecting interest. The loan was a bond. So what exactly were they holding?

mascot.line: Stocks and bonds get mixed up. A stock makes you an owner; a bond makes you a lender.

cards.headline: A bond is an IOU you can buy
cards.body: Buying a bond means lending money to whoever issued it: a government, a city or a company. In return they promise interest at a set rate, usually paid on a schedule such as every six months, and your original sum, the face value, back on a set date called maturity. Level 8 said your bank balance is the bank's IOU to you. A bond is an IOU with a price tag.

cards.headline: Steadier than stocks, not risk-free
cards.body: Bonds can bring a predictable income and help offset jumpier stocks. But the issuer might fail to pay: that's a default. If a company goes bust, its bondholders are paid before its shareholders, who get whatever is left, which may be nothing. Selling early has a catch too. When interest rates rise, new bonds pay more, so an older, lower-paying bond may only sell at a discount.

cards.fact: Britain's War Loan had no end date, until the government picked one.
cards.context: In 1932, holders of the 5% War Loan from 1917 were persuaded to switch to a lower-paying 3½% bond with no fixed maturity. That let the government choose when to repay. It waited until 2015, when interest rates were exceptionally low, and paid off the £1.9 billion still outstanding.

title: Stock Markets
objective: After this level you can explain how stock exchanges match buyers and sellers.
summary: The NYSE grew from the 1792 Buttonwood Agreement. Exchanges gather buyers and sellers so you can nearly always trade; bids and asks meet, and orders are matched automatically.

cards.headline: The New York Stock Exchange began as a two-sentence deal between 24 brokers.
cards.body: They signed it on May 17, 1792, meeting under a buttonwood tree on Wall Street, and promised to trade with each other at fixed commissions. The tree is long gone. Its job, bringing buyers and sellers together, is bigger than ever.

cards.headline: The problem an exchange solves
cards.body: Say you want to sell a share. Somewhere there's a buyer, but where? Remember Level 2's mechanic hunting for a farmer with a broken car? An exchange ends the hunt by bringing buyers and sellers together in one place. It guarantees a basic level of liquidity: you can always find someone to trade with. Whether you like their price is another story.

cards.headline: Bids, asks and the spread
cards.body: Every stock has two live prices. The bid is the highest price any buyer will pay; the ask is the lowest any seller will take. The ask is almost always higher, and the gap between them is the spread. Electronic networks match buy and sell orders automatically. The price in the headlines is the last trade, not a promise about yours.

cards.headline: Speed or price: pick one
cards.body: A market order says: trade now. It's sure to go through, but the price isn't guaranteed. A limit order says: only at my price or better, so a buy fills at your limit or lower and a sell at your limit or higher. Your price is protected, but the trade might never happen.

title: Diversification
objective: After this level you can explain why spreading money across many investments lowers risk.
summary: Diversification spreads money across and within kinds of investments so one failure can't sink you. It can't prevent losses in a market-wide fall. Enron's workers showed the cost of one basket.

cards.headline: At Enron, many workers kept their paycheck and their savings in one basket.
cards.body: At the end of 2000, more than half the money in Enron's 401(k) retirement plan was invested in Enron's own stock. On December 2, 2001, the company went bankrupt. Many employees lost their jobs and much of their retirement savings at the same moment.

cards.headline: Don't put all your eggs in one basket
cards.body: That old saying is the whole idea of diversification: spreading your money among different investments to reduce risk. If one company or industry does badly, others doing well may make up for it. You can spread across kinds of assets, like stocks, bonds and cash, and within them: many companies, in many different industries.

cards.headline: What spreading out can't do
cards.body: Diversification shrinks the damage any single failure can do. It can't make you immune when the whole market drops. It improves the odds that you won't lose money, or won't lose as much, but it guarantees nothing. Remember Level 32's 1931, when US stocks lost more than 40%? Owning every one of them wouldn't have saved you that year.

cards.fact: Funds make spreading out easy.
cards.context: Buying hundreds of companies one at a time would be a lot of paperwork. Mutual funds and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) pool money from many investors and invest it in many holdings, so each investor owns a small portion of all of them. One warning: a fund focused on a single industry is still one basket.

title: Index Funds
objective: After this level you can explain what index funds are and why they are popular.
summary: An index fund tracks a market index such as the S&P 500 instead of picking stocks, and can cost less. Mocked as 'Bogle's Folly' in 1976, index funds led US fund assets by 2023.

cards.headline: In 1976, a fund that didn't try to beat the market was called 'Bogle's Folly'.
cards.body: John Bogle's First Index Investment Trust hoped to raise up to $150 million. It raised about $11 million. Critics called it a path to mediocrity. Yet at the end of 2023, index-style funds in the US held more money than traditional stock-picking funds for the first time. What were they on to?

cards.headline: Buy the whole basket
cards.body: A market index, like the S&P 500, measures how a basket of investments performs. You can't buy an index itself, but an index fund can track it by holding all (or a sample) of what's inside. Instead of hunting for tomorrow's winners, it simply owns the basket. And since a fund gives each investor a small slice of many holdings, Level 36's diversification comes built in.

cards.headline: Why cheap matters
cards.body: Index funds are usually passive: they buy and sell rarely. Active funds trade more, trying to beat an index. With no research analysts picking stocks, an index fund can cost less to run, though not every one does. And fees come straight out of your return: if two funds' holdings perform the same, the cheaper fund returns more.

cards.fact: Over 15 years, 89.5% of active large-company funds trailed the index.

summary: Time does most of the work in retirement saving: the earlier you start, the longer growth earns growth. Pensions promise a benefit; in 401(k)-style plans, the worker carries the risk.

cards.headline: Skip a $1 candy bar every day for a year. What is that $365 worth in 30 years?
cards.body: The US Securities and Exchange Commission ran the numbers. Save the $365 once, let it earn 5% a year, and it grows to $465.84 in five years. Leave it alone for 30 years and it becomes $1,577.50. Same candy bars, very different payoff.

cards.headline: Time does the heavy lifting

Same money, same rate: the difference is time, because growth keeps earning growth of its own. That's why the SEC's guide for people starting their first job says starting early is key: the younger you are when you begin, the more time your investments have to grow.

In a 401(k)-style plan, the account is yours: you choose how much to save and how it's invested, and some employers add a match, such as 50 cents per dollar. title: Property and Other Assets
objective: After this level you can describe property, commodities and the other things people invest in.
summary: Investments pay through income, a price change or both. Property earns rent and changes in value; commodities trade through futures, as at Osaka's Dojima rice market; gold pays no income.

cards.headline: In 1730, Osaka's rice traders were licensed to trade rice for the future.
cards.body: In Edo-period Japan, rice collected as tax was sold to brokers for rice bills, notes you could swap for rice, and those bills were traded busily. In 1730 the shogunate authorized the Dojima Rice Exchange, with a futures market in rice. Stocks and bonds aren't the only things people invest in.

cards.headline: Two ways anything can pay
cards.body: An investment is anything you acquire to make a gain through income or a rise in value. So ask any asset two questions. Does it pay income along the way? Stocks may pay dividends; bonds pay interest. And will its price change? Total return is the income plus the price gain, or minus the loss. Those two questions sort almost everything.

cards.headline: Property: rent and price
cards.body: Property can pay both ways: buildings can produce rent, and their value can rise or fall. Buying a whole building is a big step, so there's another route. A real estate investment trust, or REIT, is a company that owns income-producing property like offices, apartments and warehouses, letting investors share the income. Some REITs trade on stock exchanges; others are illiquid and hard to sell quickly.

cards.headline: Commodities: price, and only price
cards.body: Commodities include metals, grains and other foods. Level 3's salt was one. Many now trade through futures contracts, agreements to buy or sell a set amount at a set price on a future date, just as Dojima traded rice. Some pay no income at all: gold earns no dividends or interest, so its return depends on someone paying more later. US regulators warn that precious metals are highly volatile.

title: What a Market Is
objective: After this level you can explain a market as any place where buyers and sellers meet.
summary: A market is any way buyers and sellers get in contact to trade, from a village grocer to a website. eBay's first sale, a broken laser pointer, shows how a big market finds a buyer for almost anything.

cards.headline: In 1995, a broken laser pointer sold online for $14.83.
cards.body: It didn't work, and somebody paid for it anyway. That sale was the first on the website that became eBay. To see why it makes sense, you need to know what a market really is.

cards.headline: A meeting, not a place
cards.body: Picture a market and you probably see stalls and shouting. Economists mean something wider: any way buyers and sellers get in contact to swap goods and services, face to face or through go-betweens. A village grocer counts. So does a website. In a modern economy, the market isn't a place at all. It's wherever sellers compete for your money.

cards.headline: The laser pointer finds its buyer
cards.body: Pierre Omidyar launched AuctionWeb over Labor Day weekend in 1995, and his broken laser pointer sold for $14.83. Remember Level 2's mechanic hunting for a farmer with a broken car? Omidyar had no such problem. The buyer paid in money, so Omidyar didn't need anything the buyer owned. He needed just one person, anywhere, who wanted a broken laser pointer. A big enough market finds that person.

cards.fact: Markets trade far more than things. There are markets for work and for savings.
cards.context: Supply and demand, this chapter's big idea, work in any market. In a labor market, job seekers supply work and employers demand it. In a financial market, savers supply money and borrowers demand it. And as trade in goods grew, financial markets like stock exchanges multiplied too.

title: Supply
objective: After this level you can explain why sellers offer more of something when its price rises.
summary: The law of supply: a higher price almost always brings more to market, because it means more profit. The supply curve slopes upward; costs, weather, technology and policy shift it.

cards.headline: Cookies suddenly sell for twice as much. How many do you bake?
cards.body: If you ran a bakery, you'd probably bake more, maybe stay open later. So would the bakery down the road. Economists turned that hunch into a law.

cards.headline: The law of supply
cards.body: A rise in price almost always leads sellers to offer more of a good or service, and a fall in price leads them to offer less. The amount they offer at a given price is the quantity supplied. Why the rise? A higher price means more profit, which encourages profit-seeking firms to expand production and bring more to market. More money on the table, more cookies on the shelf.

cards.headline: The curve that climbs
cards.body: Economists draw this as a supply curve: price up the side, quantity along the bottom. It usually slopes upward, like a staircase, because each higher price coaxes out more of the product. Every point on it answers one question: at this price, how much would sellers bring to Level 41's market?

cards.fact: Price isn't the only thing that moves supply.
cards.context: The curve assumes all other things stay equal, which economists call ceteris paribus. When they don't, the whole curve shifts. Supply depends on the costs of production: pricier raw materials, new taxes and bad weather for farmers cut it; better technology or a subsidy raises it. A change in the product's own price just moves sellers along the curve.

title: Demand
objective: After this level you can explain why buyers want less of something when its price rises.
summary: The law of demand: a higher price almost always cuts the quantity demanded, through the substitution and income effects. Income, tastes and related prices shift the whole demand curve.

cards.headline: When gas prices jump, people start carpooling.
cards.body: Nobody orders them to. They combine errands, take the bus and plan trips closer to home. Each person quietly buys a bit less. Add them all up and you get a law of economics.

cards.headline: The law of demand
cards.body: A rise in price almost always cuts the quantity demanded, the amount buyers want at that price. A fall in price raises it. It's Level 42's law in the mirror: when prices climb, sellers want to sell more and buyers want to buy less. Draw it and the demand curve slopes downward, because people buy more when things are cheaper.

mascot.line: Easy to blur these two: substitution is switching to cheaper things; income is your pay buying less.

cards.headline: Two reasons you buy less
cards.body: First, the substitution effect: when one thing gets pricier, you switch toward things that are now relatively cheaper, like the bus instead of the car. Second, the income effect: a higher price shrinks what your money can buy, even though your pay hasn't changed, so you buy less of most goods. Two effects, one direction.

cards.fact: Demand can change even when the price stands still.
cards.context: Like supply, the demand curve holds other things equal. Change them and the whole curve shifts: income, tastes, the prices of related goods, population, even expectations about the future. A change in the good's own price just slides buyers along the curve, exactly as Level 42's sellers slide along theirs.

title: Where Prices Come From
objective: After this level you can explain how supply and demand together set a price.
summary: The equilibrium price is where supply and demand cross. A surplus pushes prices down and a shortage pushes them up. Marshall called supply and demand the two blades of a pair of scissors.

cards.headline: Who decides what things cost?
cards.body: Most of the time, no single person. In markets, prices come from supply and demand pushing against each other. Put Level 42 and Level 43 on one chart and watch what happens.

cards.headline: Where the curves cross
cards.body: Supply climbs, demand falls, so the two curves cross at one point. That's the equilibrium price: the only price where the amount buyers want to buy equals the amount sellers want to sell. At that price, every buyer willing to pay it finds a seller, and every seller willing to accept it finds a buyer.

cards.headline: The market's nudge
cards.body: Price too high? Sellers bring more than buyers want: a surplus. Rather than sit on unsold stock, some sellers cut their prices, because selling cheaper beats not selling at all. Price too low? Buyers want more than there is: a shortage, and sellers spot a chance to charge more. Either way, the price gets shoved toward the crossing point.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing: price comes from supply and demand together, like two blades.

cards.fact: Supply or demand: which one sets the price? Both, like scissors.
cards.context: In his Principles of Economics, published in 1890, Alfred Marshall said that arguing over it is like arguing whether the upper or the lower blade of a pair of scissors does the cutting. One blade alone cuts nothing. Price comes from supply and demand working together.

title: Shortages and Surpluses
objective: After this level you can explain what happens when prices are held too low or too high.
summary: A price floor above equilibrium creates a surplus, like Europe's butter mountains. A price ceiling below equilibrium creates a shortage, like rent control.

cards.headline: In the 1980s, Europe had a butter mountain. And a wine lake.
cards.body: Those were the nicknames for giant stored surpluses of butter and wine. They grew out of a rule that stopped prices doing Level 44's job.

cards.headline: Floors make surpluses
cards.body: Governments sometimes regulate prices by law. A price floor is the lowest price anyone may legally pay. Set it above the equilibrium price and sellers offer more than buyers want: a surplus. Level 44's cure, cutting the price, is now against the rules. So the extra has nowhere to go.

cards.fact: Europe's farm policy held prices high, and farmers produced more and more.
cards.context: When the Common Agricultural Policy began in 1962, it supported farmers mainly by keeping their prices artificially high. That's a floor, and Level 42 predicts the rest: a higher price, more supply. By the 1980s, the result was huge stored surpluses of butter and wine. (The wine was actually industrial alcohol. No lake of fine vintage, sadly.)

mascot.line: Floors and ceilings get swapped all the time. A floor above equilibrium makes a surplus; a ceiling below, a shortage.

cards.headline: Ceilings make shortages
cards.body: Now flip it. A price ceiling is the highest price anyone may legally charge, often set to keep necessities affordable. Set it below equilibrium and buyers want more than sellers offer: a shortage. This time the price can't rise to close the gap, so the shortage stays. Rent control is the classic case: it can leave fewer apartments to rent than there would be at market rates.

title: Competition
objective: After this level you can explain how competition pushes prices down and quality up.
summary: In perfect competition, each seller is a price taker. Profits attract new rivals, which pushes prices down. Competition keeps prices down and quality up.

cards.headline: Try selling your corn above the market price. Watch what happens.
cards.body: Nothing happens. That's the problem: no buyers come at all. Meet the quiet force that works for you every time you shop.

cards.headline: Price takers
cards.body: In perfect competition, many firms sell identical products to many buyers, everyone knows the prices, and firms can come and go freely. A single corn farmer can't pick her price: supply and demand across the whole market set it. Ask more and buyers get the same corn from somebody else. Economists call her a price taker. The market names the price; she just takes it.

cards.headline: Profits attract rivals
cards.body: So what stops a whole industry charging a fortune? Newcomers. When sellers in a competitive market earn fat profits, new firms pile in. Their extra supply brings the price down, until the extra profit is squeezed away and nobody else wants to join. High profits are an open invitation.

cards.fact: Competition keeps prices down and quality up.
cards.context: That's how the US Federal Trade Commission puts it. When businesses must compete for your money, they have strong incentives to run efficiently, keep prices down and keep quality up. For shoppers, that adds up to lower prices, better products and services, more choice and more new ideas.

title: Monopolies
objective: After this level you can explain what a monopoly is and why governments limit them.
summary: A monopoly is one seller of something with no substitute, shielded by barriers to entry. It sells less at a higher price, so laws limit it: Standard Oil was broken up in 1911.

cards.headline: The board game Monopoly began as an economics lesson.
cards.body: It grew out of The Landlord's Game, which Lizzie Magie patented in 1904 to teach economic ideas about land and rent. Real monopolies are a lot less fun to play against.

cards.headline: One seller, no substitute
cards.body: A monopoly is a market with a single supplier of something that has no substitute. It can set its price without fear of competitors. What keeps rivals out? Barriers to entry: legal, technological or market forces that stop newcomers. Behind those walls, big profits no longer pull in Level 46's rivals, so nothing drags the price down.

cards.headline: Less stuff, higher prices
cards.body: Compared with a competitive market, a monopoly sells a smaller quantity at a higher price, so buyers lose out. It can get lazy, too: with no rival to fear, it can keep making the same old products in the same old way. In 1935, economist John Hicks summed it up: "The best of all monopoly profits is a quiet life."

cards.fact: Standard Oil once refined 90 to 95 percent of America's oil. Then came the breakup.
cards.context: That was its share by 1880. In 1890, the Sherman Act outlawed monopolizing a market, and in 1911 the US Supreme Court ordered Standard Oil broken up into separate companies. Governments limit monopolies to protect what Level 46 showed: competition is what keeps prices down and quality up.

title: Incentives
objective: After this level you can explain how incentives shape the choices people make.
summary: Incentives are rewards and penalties that shape choices, and people respond to them. Hanoi's 1902 rat-tail bounty backfired: people bred rats for their tails. Prices are incentives too.

cards.headline: In 1902, Hanoi paid people for dead rats. Soon, people were farming rats.
cards.body: It's one of history's great backfires. And it shows just how seriously people take a reward.

cards.headline: Carrots and sticks
cards.body: An incentive rewards or penalizes a choice. Positive incentives are rewards, like a buy-one-get-one-free sale. Negative incentives are penalties, like a speeding ticket or a littering fine. Some come from governments, some from businesses. People respond to them, and usually in predictable ways. That's the whole point of having them.

mascot.line: The lesson: people respond to exactly what you reward. Pay for tails, get tails.

cards.headline: The rat-tail bounty
cards.body: In colonial Hanoi, the French authorities wanted fewer rats. They paid a few cents for each rat tail handed in to the police. A tail seemed like proof of a dead rat. It wasn't. People cut the tails off rats and let them go free to breed more. Officials even found people farming rats, and a network smuggling them into the city.

cards.fact: Every price is an incentive.
cards.context: Economic incentives involve a financial benefit or cost. That's Level 42 in one line: a higher price rewards producing more, so sellers bring more to market. Hanoi's bounty was simply a price for rat tails, and people supplied rat tails. The lesson: reward exactly what you want, because that's what you'll get.

title: Scarcity
objective: After this level you can explain scarcity as the basic problem that economics studies.
summary: Scarcity means wants exceed what's available, for everyone. Economics studies how people choose under scarcity. It explains why water, vital but plentiful, costs less than diamonds.

cards.headline: Water keeps you alive. Diamonds don't. Guess which costs more.
cards.body: Adam Smith puzzled over exactly this in 1776. The answer is the problem at the heart of all economics.

mascot.line: Scarce doesn't mean rare. It means not enough to go round, for everyone.

cards.headline: Wants beat what there is
cards.body: Scarcity means people's wants for goods, services and resources exceed what's available. It doesn't mean rare. It means not enough to go round, and it hits everyone. The ultimate scarce resource is time: rich or poor, you get the same 24 hours a day. No billionaire can buy a 25th.

cards.headline: The study of choosing
cards.body: Because there's never enough of everything, people have to choose. That's what economics studies: how people make decisions in the face of scarcity. In 1932, Lionel Robbins put it this way: economics studies human behavior as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses. Translation: limited stuff, many possible uses, pick.

cards.fact: Water is vital and cheap. Diamonds are useless and dear. Scarcity explains it.
cards.context: In The Wealth of Nations, Smith noted that nothing is more useful than water, yet it buys scarcely anything, while a diamond, of scarcely any use, trades for a great quantity of other goods. The standard answer: water is plentiful, so one more glass is worth little to you. Diamonds are scarce, so each one is worth a lot. Price follows scarcity, not usefulness.

title: Milestone: How Markets Work
objective: After this level you can connect money, banks, investing and markets into one picture of how an economy runs.
summary: Prices are messages that tell people what's scarce, with nobody giving orders. Money makes them readable, and supply and demand run markets for goods, work and savings alike.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Time to see the whole machine.
cards.body: Money, markets, supply, demand, competition, incentives, scarcity. They aren't separate topics. They're one machine, and the price tag is where every part of it meets.

cards.headline: Prices are messages
cards.body: In 1945, economist Friedrich Hayek asked you to imagine tin becoming scarcer, from a new use or a lost source. Tin users don't need to know which. The price rises, and they economize. Hayek called the price system a mechanism for communicating information: it gets tens of thousands of strangers to use a material more sparingly, with nobody giving orders.

cards.headline: Money makes the message readable
cards.body: Those messages need Level 1's money. As a unit of account, it puts every price on one ruler, so tin, bread and a haircut can be compared at a glance. Radford's camp showed it in miniature: once prices were quoted in cigarettes, like cheese for seven, anyone could compare anything with anything.

mascot.line: This is Level 44's scissors again, cutting in every market.

cards.headline: One machine, many markets
cards.body: The same machine runs markets you've met elsewhere in this tree. In labor markets, job seekers supply work and employers demand it. In financial markets, savers supply money and borrowers demand it, and they meet at a rate of return, like an interest rate. Banks, shares and paychecks have their own chapters, but underneath it's supply and demand, meeting at a price.

title: Taxes
objective: After this level you can explain what taxes pay for and name the main kinds of tax.
summary: Taxes pay for what governments provide, about a third of GDP across rich countries. They fall on what you earn, buy and own; most countries use a VAT, the US does not.

cards.headline: In 1789, Benjamin Franklin named the only two sure things in life.
cards.body: One was death. The other was taxes. More than two centuries later, both are still going strong. So what do they actually pay for, and what exactly gets taxed?

cards.headline: What your taxes buy
cards.body: Taxes are how a government pays for the things it provides. In the US, the biggest federal items are national defense, Social Security, healthcare and interest on past borrowing. States and cities spend most on education, then on highways, libraries, parks, police and fire protection. So the fire truck racing down your street? You've already chipped in.

cards.fact: Across rich countries, taxes add up to about a third of the whole economy.
cards.context: In 2023, taxes averaged 33.9% of GDP (the value of everything a country produces in a year) across OECD countries. The range is wide: under a fifth in Mexico, over two-fifths in France and Denmark. How big that slice should be is a choice each country makes, and they choose very differently.

cards.context: A value-added tax is a sales tax collected in slices. Each business along the chain, from lumber yard to furniture maker, pays tax on its sales and gets credit for the tax already paid on its inputs. More than 170 countries use one. The US relies instead on state and local sales taxes, added at the till.
