title: Who Pays What
objective: After this level you can compare tax systems where the rate rises with income to systems with one rate.
summary: Progressive taxes take a bigger share of bigger incomes, flat taxes the same share, regressive taxes a smaller share. Brackets tax only the extra dollars, so a raise never cuts your pay.

cards.headline: Could a raise push you into a higher tax bracket and leave you poorer?
cards.body: No. Only the extra dollars pay the higher rate, so your take-home pay still rises. Why that's true opens up the bigger question of this level: how should a tax bill be shared out?

cards.headline: Three ways to share the bill
cards.body: Picture three people earning very different incomes. A progressive tax takes a bigger share from the higher incomes; the US federal income tax works this way. A proportional, or flat, tax takes the same share from everyone, like the US Medicare payroll tax. A regressive tax takes a smaller share as income rises. In 1994, Estonia became the first country in Eastern Europe to swap its income tax for a flat one.

mascot.line: A stubborn myth: a raise can shrink your take-home pay. It can't; only the extra dollars pay more.

cards.headline: Brackets are buckets
cards.body: Progressive income taxes usually work in brackets. Picture your income pouring into a row of buckets. The first bucket is taxed at the lowest rate; only the money that spills into the next bucket pays the next rate, and so on. So when a raise tips you into a higher bracket, only the extra dollars are taxed at the higher rate. Your take-home pay goes up. Always.
cards.callout: A higher bracket taxes the extra dollars, not all of them.

cards.headline: The same rate, a different bite
cards.body: Remember Level 51's taxes on what you buy? A sales tax charges everyone the same rate at the till. But lower-income households spend a bigger share of their income on goods, while higher-income households spend a smaller share of theirs. So measured against income, a sales tax takes a bigger bite from lower incomes. That makes it regressive, even though the rate never changes.

title: Public Goods
objective: After this level you can explain why things like roads and lighthouses are usually paid for by governments.
summary: Public goods are nonexcludable and nonrival, so people can free ride and markets underprovide them. Taxes fix that. Coase found England's lighthouses were paid for by port dues.

cards.headline: Economists' go-to example for a century: the lighthouse. Then someone checked.
cards.body: From John Stuart Mill to Paul Samuelson, the lighthouse stood for something markets supposedly couldn't provide: how would you make a passing ship pay for the light? To see the problem, start with a fireworks show.

cards.headline: The fireworks problem
cards.body: Someone has to pay for the town's fireworks show. But once the rockets go up, anyone can watch from their own backyard. So each person has a reason to let others pay and enjoy the show for free. Economists call that free riding. If enough people do it, the money never comes in, and a show everyone would have enjoyed simply never happens.

cards.headline: Public goods
cards.body: Fireworks are a public good, with two features. They're nonexcludable: it's costly or impossible to stop non-payers from enjoying them. And they're nonrival: your watching doesn't use up anyone else's view. National defense is the classic case, protecting everyone in a country at once. The usual fix is the one from Level 51: people agree through politics to pay taxes for it, and the free riders have nowhere to hide.

cards.fact: England's early lighthouses were often privately run, paid for by fees collected at ports.
cards.context: In 1974, economist Ronald Coase dug into the history. Ships that passed a light still had to dock somewhere, and there they paid light dues. Free riding solved? Critics point out that the right to collect those dues came from a royal patent, so government was still doing the enforcing. The lighthouse turned out to be a debate, not a textbook certainty.

title: Government Budgets and Debt
objective: After this level you can explain deficits, surpluses and national debt.
summary: A deficit is one year's gap between spending and taxes; the national debt is the running total of borrowing plus interest. Economists weigh its risks and uses differently.

cards.headline: In 2015, Britain paid off debts from the 1700s.
cards.body: Some of the old bonds it repaid traced back to the South Sea Bubble crash of 1720 and to borrowing used for the Napoleonic Wars. How does a country end up owing money for nearly three centuries? Start with a single year's budget.

cards.headline: Deficit or surplus
cards.body: Every year, a government compares what it spends with what it collects in taxes. Spend more than it collects, and it runs a budget deficit. Collect more than it spends, and it runs a surplus. If the two match, the budget is balanced. Surpluses don't come around often: the US federal government last ran one in 2001.

mascot.line: Deficit and debt get mixed up constantly. The deficit is the tap; the debt is the water level.

cards.headline: The bathtub
cards.body: A deficit is one year's gap; the debt is the running total. To cover a deficit, a government borrows, largely by selling bonds. The national debt is all that borrowing added up, plus the interest owed. Think of a bathtub: the deficit is the tap running this year, the debt is the water level. Borrow $10,000 a year for four years and your yearly deficit is $10,000, but your debt is $40,000.

title: Central Banks
objective: After this level you can explain what a central bank does and why it is kept independent.
summary: Central banks run monetary policy and watch over banks. Sweden's Riksbank (1668) is the oldest. They are kept independent from elections, though critics question unelected power.

cards.headline: The world's oldest central bank rose from the ruins of a failed one.
cards.body: Remember Level 5's Stockholms Banco, which issued Europe's first banknotes in 1661 and failed when the public lost confidence? Its founder, Johan Palmstruch, was sentenced to death, then reprieved. And in 1668, Sweden built a new bank from the wreckage. It still runs today as the Riksbank.

cards.headline: The bank at the center
cards.body: A central bank is the bank at the heart of a country's money. The US got one, the Federal Reserve, in 1913. Its jobs include steering interest rates and money (monetary policy), supervising banks, keeping the financial system stable and payments safe. Since 1977, Congress has told it to aim for maximum employment and stable prices. The goal is old: the Riksbank's law told it to keep the coinage at its 'right and fair value' from 1668.

cards.headline: Why keep it at arm's length?
cards.body: Imagine an election is coming. A government may be tempted to juice the economy with cheap money, even if prices rise later. So many countries put money decisions at arm's length. Federal Reserve governors serve staggered 14-year terms, and elected officials can't sit on its Board. A study of 155 central banks over 50 years found that greater independence helped keep inflation in check.

cards.headline: Independent, but answerable
cards.body: Not everyone is comfortable. Critics question whether unelected officials should hold so much power over everyone's money. Paul Tucker, a former Bank of England deputy governor, explored exactly that in his 2018 book, Unelected Power. The usual answer is accountability: the Fed's chair testifies to Congress, and it reports on its policy twice a year. Where to draw the line is still argued over.

title: Interest Rates and the Economy
objective: After this level you can explain how central banks raise or lower interest rates to cool or boost the economy.
summary: A central bank's key rate feeds into loan and savings rates. Raising it cools spending and price rises; cutting it boosts borrowing and hiring. Effects lag. Volcker's near-20% rates show the cost.

cards.headline: In 1981, America's key interest rate was near 20%. On purpose.
cards.body: Under chair Paul Volcker, the Federal Reserve let the federal funds rate approach 20% to fight high inflation. Why would a central bank make borrowing that painful? Follow what one interest rate does to a whole economy.

cards.headline: One rate, many ripples
cards.body: A central bank sets one core short-term interest rate: the Bank of England calls its version Bank Rate. It sounds like a number only bankers care about, but it ripples outward. Change it, and the rates banks charge on loans and mortgages, and pay on savings, tend to follow. Your mortgage, your car loan and your savings account all feel it.

cards.headline: The brake and the accelerator
cards.body: Raising the rate is the brake. Loan and mortgage payments go up and saving pays more, so people spend less, and businesses find it harder to raise prices. Cutting the rate is the accelerator. Borrowing gets cheaper, so households and businesses spend more, and businesses hire more workers to keep up.

cards.headline: A shower with a long pipe
cards.body: The catch is timing. In 1959, economist Milton Friedman told Congress that monetary policy works with a long and variable lag; in his study, the delay ran from 4 to 29 months. It's like a shower with a very long pipe: turn the tap, wait, and it's easy to overshoot into scalding or freezing before you feel the change.

cards.fact: Volcker's brake slowed prices, and it hurt.
cards.context: High rates hit industries that run on borrowing, like construction and autos. US unemployment reached nearly 11% late in 1982. But by October 1982, inflation had fallen to 5%. The brake worked on one goal while hurting another.

title: Printing Money
objective: After this level you can explain why creating money too fast makes prices rise.
summary: When money grows faster than the goods it buys, prices rise, as in Radford's camp and 16th-century Europe. The link holds over time but is not mechanical.

cards.headline: In Level 1's prison camp, a flood of cigarettes sent prices soaring.
cards.body: Economist R. A. Radford saw it happen. Big deliveries could bring several hundred thousand cigarettes within a fortnight. Prices soared, then fell as stocks ran out. The camp's money had suddenly multiplied. What does that do to prices?

cards.headline: More money, same stuff
cards.body: Why would more money push prices up? Picture a market with the same bread and jam as yesterday, but everyone holding twice the cash. The quantity theory of money says that when money grows faster than the goods and services it can buy, the extra money bids up prices rather than conjuring more stuff. Milton Friedman's answer was a rule: if output grows 2% a year, let money grow 2% too, and prices stay put.

cards.fact: In the 1500s, a flood of American silver helped push up European prices.
cards.context: From 1550, silver from mines like Potosí arrived in Spain in huge volumes and spread across Europe. Over the century, prices rose about sixfold, in what historians call the price revolution. They also point to a growing population needing food and housing, and still debate how much each cause mattered.

cards.headline: Not a simple dial
cards.body: The link isn't a machine. In the 1980s and 1990s, how fast money changed hands became unstable, and many economists dropped strict money-growth rules. Most still agree prices can't keep rising indefinitely without more money. And today's 'printing' rarely needs a press: remember Level 8, where 97% of the money UK people hold is bank deposits.

title: Rules for Business
objective: After this level you can explain why governments set rules for banks and businesses.
summary: Rules help where sellers know more than buyers, as The Jungle showed in 1906, and make banks hold capital to absorb losses. Every rule also has costs, which is why the right amount is argued over.

cards.headline: A 1906 novel turned readers' stomachs and changed the law that same year.
cards.body: Upton Sinclair's The Jungle showed filthy conditions in Chicago's meatpacking plants. On June 30, 1906, President Theodore Roosevelt signed both the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act. Why did buyers need a law to protect them?

cards.headline: You can't see inside a sausage
cards.body: The seller knows how it was made; you don't. Economists call this asymmetric information: one side of a deal knows more about quality than the other. Rules help close the gap. The 1906 food law banned adulterated and mislabeled food and drugs from being shipped between states. US advertising rules let sellers exaggerate, but a claim presented as a fact must be true.

cards.headline: A cushion for banks
cards.body: Banks get rules too. Regulators make them hold capital: the owners' own money, which works like a cushion. If some loans go bad, the losses hit that cushion first, so the bank can still repay its depositors. The aim is to make bank failures, and government bailouts, less likely.

title: Safety Nets
objective: After this level you can explain unemployment insurance, pensions and other safety nets.
summary: Germany created old-age social insurance in 1889. Unemployment insurance replaces part of lost wages. US Social Security is pay-as-you-go, strained as workers per beneficiary fall.

cards.headline: The world's first state pension started at age 70.
cards.body: In 1889, Germany, under Chancellor Otto von Bismarck, became the first nation to adopt old-age social insurance. It gave workers basic security from age 70, and workers, employers and the government all paid in. It was a net stretched under ordinary life.

cards.headline: Insurance for losing your job
cards.body: A safety net catches you when income suddenly stops. Unemployment insurance gives temporary, partial wage replacement to workers who lose their jobs through no fault of their own. Temporary, because it runs out; partial, because it covers only part of your old pay. In between, it helps people keep paying the rent and the bills while they look for work.

cards.headline: Today's workers, today's retirees
cards.body: US Social Security is one of Level 51's biggest federal items, and it works pay-as-you-go. The taxes today's workers pay fund today's beneficiaries; nobody's contributions sit in a personal pot. That makes one ratio matter a lot. In 1965, about four workers paid in for each beneficiary. By 2023, there were 2.7.

title: What Inflation Is
objective: After this level you can explain inflation as a general rise in prices over time.
summary: Inflation is a broad rise in prices that shrinks what money buys. Its causes include demand-pull, cost-push and expectations; economists disagree on how much money supply matters.

cards.headline: In Level 1's prison camp, a flood of cigarettes sent prices soaring.
cards.body: Radford watched it happen: several hundred thousand cigarettes might arrive in a fortnight. Prices soared, then fell back as stocks ran out. The camp had just lived through a small, smoky bout of inflation.

mascot.line: Keep this: inflation means prices in general, not one item. The next few levels build on it.

cards.headline: Prices, plural
cards.body: Inflation is the rate at which prices rise over a period of time. The key word is broad: it tracks the overall rise in prices across a country, not one item. If only coffee gets pricier after a bad harvest, that's coffee news. When the whole shopping list creeps up together, month after month, that's inflation.

cards.fact: Inflation shrinks your money without changing the number on it.
cards.context: Economists call it lost purchasing power: as prices rise, each unit of money buys less. That's a blow to Level 1's third job, store of value. A banknote in a drawer shows the same amount next year; it just buys less. And if your pay rises more slowly than prices, you can afford less, even after a raise.

cards.headline: Why prices rise, and why economists argue
cards.body: Textbooks name three culprits. Demand-pull: spending outgrows what the economy can produce, "too much money chasing too few goods." Cost-push: a shock like pricier oil raises the cost of making things. Expectations: if everyone expects higher prices, wages and contracts build them in. How much each matters is argued over. Milton Friedman said inflation is "always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon"; Keynesians put more weight on spending and demand.

title: Measuring Inflation
objective: After this level you can explain how a basket of everyday goods measures the cost of living.
summary: The consumer price index tracks the cost of a spending-weighted basket of what households buy. The basket is updated as habits change, and a fixed basket tends to overstate how fast living costs rise.

cards.headline: In 2024, air fryers were officially promoted into Britain's inflation basket.
cards.body: Vinyl records got back in too. Hand sanitiser got dropped. To measure inflation, statisticians track a whole basket of what people buy, and they keep repacking it.

cards.headline: A country-sized shopping cart
cards.body: The consumer price index, or CPI, tracks the cost of a representative basket of goods and services that households buy. Its rise is how inflation gets measured. In the US, data collectors record the prices of about 80,000 items every month. Each item counts in proportion to what households actually spend on it, so housing, the biggest slice, far outweighs clothing.

cards.headline: The basket gets repacked
cards.body: A basket frozen in time would slowly stop looking like real life. So the UK updates its basket, 744 items in 2024, every year. That year, air fryers went in, prized for their energy savings, and vinyl records returned after more than thirty years away. Hand sanitiser came out as the pandemic faded. The basket is a portrait of how people live, redrawn every year.

cards.headline: Why a fixed basket runs hot
cards.body: Say beef gets pricey, so you switch to chicken. A fixed basket assumes you kept buying beef, so it overstates how much your living costs rose. That's substitution bias. A fixed basket also misses quality: a new phone that does more for the same price looks like no change at all. Both quirks make a fixed basket overstate the rising cost of living, which is why US statisticians now use methods that allow for some switching.

title: Hyperinflation
objective: After this level you can describe hyperinflation in Weimar Germany and Zimbabwe and explain what caused it.
summary: Hyperinflation is inflation above 50% a month. Weimar Germany in 1923 and Zimbabwe in 2008 both printed money to pay the government's bills until their currencies collapsed.

cards.headline: In 1914, a dollar cost just over four German marks. By late 1923: trillions.
cards.body: About 4.2 trillion, to be exact. That isn't prices creeping up. That's money dissolving, and economists have a name for it.

cards.headline: When inflation runs wild
cards.body: In 1956, economist Phillip Cagan drew the line: hyperinflation means prices rising more than 50% in a single month. It usually starts the same way. A government creates new money to pay for its spending, faster than the economy can produce. Then trust breaks. People rush to spend money before it loses more value, or swap it for foreign currency, and prices race even faster.

cards.headline: Germany, 1923
cards.body: After World War I, Germany's government printed more and more money to pay its bills, including war reparations. In early 1923, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr region, coal output there stopped, and prices climbed further. Savings were wiped out. Historians still debate the blame: how much lies with reparations, and how much with Germany's own choices, such as printing money rather than raising taxes.

cards.fact: In 2008, Zimbabwe's prices were doubling roughly every day.
cards.context: After land reforms crippled farm output, Zimbabwe's government printed money aggressively. By mid-November 2008, monthly inflation hit about 79.6 billion percent. In January 2009, a 100 trillion dollar note went into circulation. That same year, the country gave up its own currency, and people paid in foreign money, mainly US dollars.

title: Deflation
objective: After this level you can explain why falling prices can hurt an economy.
summary: Deflation is a general fall in prices. It usually comes from collapsing spending, and it hurts by making people delay purchases and making debts heavier.

cards.headline: Prices that keep falling sound like a never-ending sale. Economists dread them.
cards.body: Level 1's camp got a taste. When cigarette deliveries stopped, stocks ran out and prices fell. Trade slid back toward barter. Some sale.

cards.headline: Deflation, defined
cards.body: Deflation is a general decline in prices, and as Fed governor Ben Bernanke stressed in 2002, the key word is general. TVs getting cheaper because factories got more efficient is generally no problem for the economy as a whole. Real deflation is almost always a side effect of a collapse in spending so severe that producers must keep cutting prices to find buyers.

cards.headline: Why buy today?
cards.body: If prices will be lower next month, why buy now? When prices are falling, people delay purchases if they can. Multiply that across a whole country and you get less economic activity, less income for the businesses selling things, and slower growth. A sale that makes everyone wait turns into a stall.

mascot.line: Keep this: the number on your loan stays put. What each of those dollars is worth goes up.

cards.fact: Under deflation, debts get heavier while you sleep.
cards.context: A loan is a fixed amount of money. When prices fall, each dollar is worth more, so borrowers repay dollars of ever-increasing real value. Japan showed how stubborn this can be: by 2002, a mild fall in consumer prices, about 1% a year, had come with years of painfully slow growth.

title: GDP
objective: After this level you can explain what GDP measures and what it misses.
summary: GDP adds up the market value of the final goods and services a country produces. Real GDP strips out price changes, and GDP misses unpaid work, pollution, leisure and how income is shared.

cards.headline: Cook dinner at home and GDP ignores it. Buy the same meal, and it counts.
cards.body: Same food, same full stomach. The economy's headline number sees only one of them. What it counts, and what it skips, is this level's story.

cards.headline: Everything a country makes, in one number
cards.body: Gross domestic product, or GDP, is the market value of the final goods and services a country produces in a period, such as a quarter or a year. "Final" matters: flour sold to a baker is an input, and only the bread counts. You can add GDP up three ways: the value added at each stage of production, the spending of final buyers, or the incomes everyone earns making it all.

cards.headline: Real GDP: more stuff, not just pricier stuff
cards.body: Remember Level 61? If a country made exactly the same things this year but prices rose, its GDP in money terms would still grow. That's why economists watch real GDP, which adjusts for price changes. Real growth means the economy actually made more, not that the price tags got bigger.

cards.fact: The first US national accounts came with a warning label.
cards.context: In 1934, economist Simon Kuznets presented them to Congress, and warned that the welfare of a nation can scarcely be inferred from national income. GDP leaves out unpaid work like housework and volunteering, and ignores pollution, lost leisure and how income is shared. It measures how much a country produces, not how well its people live.

title: The Business Cycle
objective: After this level you can explain why economies go through booms and recessions.
summary: Economies swing irregularly between expansions and recessions, which the NBER dates after the fact. Economists debate whether spending swings or productivity shocks drive the cycle.

cards.headline: The US spent a whole year in recession before it was made official.
cards.body: On December 1, 2008, the referees announced that a recession had begun back in December 2007. Economies rise and fall, but the turns are only clear in the rear-view mirror.

cards.headline: A rollercoaster without a timetable
cards.body: Economies go through expansions, or booms, when activity grows, and recessions, when it declines. The peak is the last month of an expansion; the trough is the last month of a recession. It's called a cycle, but it keeps no schedule: expansions and recessions arrive at irregular intervals and last for different lengths of time.

cards.headline: Who calls a recession?
cards.body: In the US, the referees are the National Bureau of Economic Research, or NBER. Its definition: a significant decline in economic activity, spread across the economy, lasting more than a few months. The popular rule of two straight quarters of falling real GDP isn't the NBER's test, though most recessions fit it. Recessions vary a lot: the 2020 one lasted about two months.

cards.headline: Why the ride? Economists split
cards.body: Economists still disagree about what drives the cycle. Many see swings in spending as the main engine: a surge in private or public spending fuels a boom, and a pullback brings a recession. Central banks can push too, by raising or lowering interest rates. Economists in the new classical tradition argue instead that cycles come largely from shocks to productivity and tastes, not changes in demand.

cards.headline: You can have no job and still not count as unemployed.

cards.headline: Asking 60,000 households

You count as unemployed if you have no job, have actively looked for work in the prior 4 weeks, and are available to start. Why not just count benefit claims? Many jobless people aren't eligible or never apply.

mascot.line: Stop looking for work, and the statistics stop looking at you. That catches plenty of people out.

cards.headline: The rate, and who vanishes from it

Retirees, students and discouraged workers, who want a job but have stopped looking, sit outside the labor force. So give up looking and you vanish from the unemployment rate, even though you're still out of work.

title: Bubbles
objective: After this level you can explain speculative bubbles, from Dutch tulips to dot-com stocks.
summary: A bubble is a price far above what fundamentals justify, kept up by buyers hoping to sell higher. Tulip mania was smaller than its legend; the dot-com bubble burst in 2000.

cards.headline: In February 1637, the Dutch market for tulip bulbs cracked.
cards.body: It has long been called the first recorded speculative bubble. But what is a bubble, and was this really one? The legend and the archives disagree.

cards.headline: What makes a bubble
cards.body: A bubble is when an asset's price sits far above what its fundamentals justify, and stays there for a long time. Why would anyone overpay? Because they expect to sell to someone even more optimistic. The catch: bubbles are hard to spot while you're inside one, and many are only called bubbles in hindsight.

cards.headline: Tulips: a virus, a crash, a myth
cards.body: Dutch collectors prized "broken" tulips with striped petals. The stripes came from a virus, which made those bulbs rare and unpredictable. In February 1637 the market cracked, as many buyers said they couldn't pay the prices they had agreed. Charles Mackay's 1841 book told of everyone from merchants to chimney sweeps joining in. Historian Anne Goldgar searched the archives: few people were involved, and she couldn't find anybody who went bankrupt.

cards.headline: Dot-com: a bubble with a stock ticker
cards.body: In the late 1990s, money poured into internet start-ups, many with little to show in products or profits. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index peaked in March 2000, and by October 2002 it was down more than 78%. Were bubbles like this obvious? Economists still argue. In 2013, the Nobel went to both Robert Shiller, who argues prices can drift far from fundamentals, and Eugene Fama, pioneer of the view that markets are efficient.

title: The Great Depression

summary: From 1929, US output fell by a third and prices fell. Economists still debate the cause (the crash, a shrinking money supply, the gold standard). It reshaped economic policy.

cards.headline: In 2002, a Fed official apologized for the Great Depression.

cards.fact: Between 1929 and 1933, US output fell by about a third.
cards.context: Unemployment reached about 25% of the labor force, and thousands of banks failed, more than 1,000 a year from 1930 to 1933. Prices fell about 10% a year: Level 64's deflation at full strength. The slump lasted until about 1941, the longest and deepest downturn in US history.

cards.headline: Who did it? Economists still argue
cards.body: Economists still disagree about the cause. One story starts with the 1929 stock market crash, which destroyed wealth and scared consumers and firms into spending less. Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz blamed a shrinking money supply: as banks failed and the Fed failed to step in, money fell by nearly 30%, and spending fell with it. Others stress Level 7's gold standard, which helped spread the slump from country to country.

cards.headline: The Depression rewrote the rulebook
cards.body: The Depression sparked fundamental changes in economic institutions, policy and theory. The US got federal deposit insurance, securities regulation, Social Security and its first national minimum wage. And the Fed took the lesson personally: Bernanke's apology ended, "But thanks to you, we won't do it again."

title: Why Countries Trade
objective: After this level you can explain why trade can leave both sides better off.
summary: Voluntary trade happens only when both sides expect to gain, and countries trade because their resources and climates differ. A country gains overall, but some of its workers and firms lose.

cards.headline: Scotland could make fine wine. It would just cost about 30 times as much.
cards.body: Adam Smith pointed it out: with glass, hotbeds and heated walls, very good grapes will grow in Scotland. So why import wine at all? Answer that, and you know why countries trade.

mascot.line: Keep this: a voluntary trade happens only when both sides come out ahead.

cards.headline: Both sides win, or it doesn't happen
cards.body: Nobody forces a voluntary trade. It happens only if it makes both parties better off: you hand over something you value less for something you value more. Economists call that positive-sum. The swap doesn't just move value around; it creates some. The logic is the same in a school cafeteria and in the global marketplace. Countries don't trade to beat each other. They trade because each side comes out ahead.

cards.headline: Copper for coffee
cards.body: Countries are dealt different hands. Chile has copper; Guatemala's climate suits coffee. So Chile provides copper, Guatemala grows coffee, and they trade. Money makes the swap easy: exports bring money into a country and imports send it out. That's Level 1's medium of exchange, working across borders. Chile doesn't need a Guatemalan who wants copper, just buyers who pay.

cards.fact: Trade makes a country better off overall, not every person in it.
cards.context: Shoppers get lower prices and more variety, and exporters reach bigger markets. But some firms fail against cheaper foreign rivals, and their workers lose jobs. The gains are spread thinly across millions of people and are hard to see; the costs land hard on particular companies and workers. That's why trade can be good for a country and still be fiercely argued about.

title: Comparative Advantage
objective: After this level you can explain why countries gain by specializing, even when one is better at everything.
summary: Ricardo showed in 1817 that Portugal and England both gain by specializing, though Portugal was better at both goods. What counts is comparative advantage: the lowest cost in goods given up.

cards.headline: Portugal was better at making both wine and cloth. It should still buy cloth.
cards.body: That was David Ricardo's claim in 1817: specialization and free trade benefit all trading partners, even the less efficient ones. It sounds backwards. Let's check his numbers.

cards.headline: Ricardo's numbers: workers needed for a year

mascot.line: Absolute and comparative advantage get mixed up. Comparative is about what you give up.

cards.headline: Better at everything, cheaper at one
cards.body: Portugal has an absolute advantage in both goods: it can make more of each than England. But costs are relative. In Portugal, wine takes fewer workers than cloth (80 against 90), so wine is its bargain. In England, cloth takes fewer than wine (100 against 120), so cloth is England's. That's comparative advantage: making a good at a lower cost in terms of the other goods you give up.

cards.fact: Specialize and swap, and both countries end up with more of both.
cards.context: If Portugal makes only wine and England only cloth, then they trade, each can consume more wine and more cloth than by making both itself. Real life is messier than two countries and two goods: resources are limited, and workers and jobs don't always switch industries neatly. But the core idea holds: you don't have to be the best at something to gain from trading it.

title: Imports and Exports
objective: After this level you can explain imports, exports and the balance of trade.
summary: Exports are sold abroad and imports are bought from abroad; travel spending counts too. Exports minus imports gives the trade balance, and whether a deficit matters is debated.

cards.headline: Buy a souvenir on holiday abroad, and your country just imported something.
cards.body: No ship, no container, no customs form. Yet the statisticians count it. What foreign visitors spend in a country counts as its exports, and what its residents spend on trips abroad counts as imports.

cards.headline: Out the door, in the door
cards.body: An export is a good or service a country sells to other countries; an import is one it buys from them. Exports bring money in, and imports send it out. Goods like cars and coffee count, but so do services: finance, software, consulting and design. So does your holiday. A tourist eating pasta in Rome is, technically, an Italian export.

cards.headline: Keeping score
cards.body: Take exports, subtract imports, and you get the trade balance. Export more than you import and you run a trade surplus. Import more and you run a trade deficit. The United States has run a deficit year after year since the mid-1970s. So is it losing?

cards.fact: Is a trade deficit a loss? People disagree.
cards.context: Some policymakers see a deficit as proof that a country is losing at trade. Most experts say a deficit, or a surplus, is in itself neither good nor bad. Remember Level 71: each trade happens because both sides expect to gain. Whether a country's overall deficit is a problem is a separate, and still debated, question.

title: Tariffs
objective: After this level you can explain what tariffs are and who ends up paying them.
summary: A tariff is a tax on imports, paid by the importing company, and its cost often reaches shoppers, as with 2018's US washer tariffs. Supporters and critics weigh jobs against costs.

cards.headline: In 2018, the US put a tariff on imported washers. Dryers got pricier too.
cards.body: Dryers had no tariff at all. To see why their prices moved, you need to know what a tariff is and who ends up paying it.

mascot.line: A common mix-up: the foreign country doesn't pay the tariff. The importer does.

cards.headline: A tax at the border
cards.body: A tariff is a tax on goods as they cross a national border, usually charged by the importing country. The foreign country doesn't pay it. The importing company does, handing it to the customs authority. Then the cost moves: the importer can pass it on to shoppers as higher prices or absorb it, and foreign exporters may accept thinner profit margins to keep selling.

cards.fact: Washer prices rose about 12%. Dryers, with no tariff, rose about the same.
cards.context: Economists Aaron Flaaen, Ali Hortaçsu and Felix Tintelnot studied the 2018 tariffs. People often buy washers and dryers together, so sellers raised dryer prices too. The tariffs did create about 1,800 US jobs. The study put the cost to consumers at roughly $815,000 a year for each of those jobs.

title: Exchange Rates
objective: After this level you can explain how currencies are traded and why their values change.
summary: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another. Floating rates move with interest rates, inflation and expectations; a stronger currency makes imports cheaper and exports pricier.

cards.headline: Every day, $9.6 trillion of money is traded for other money.
cards.body: That was the daily average in April 2025, up from $7.5 trillion in 2022. It's the foreign exchange market, where people and firms use one currency to buy another. Every price in it is an exchange rate.

cards.headline: A price tag on money
cards.body: An exchange rate is how much one currency is worth in terms of another. Swap dollars for euros before a trip and you're a buyer in this market. So are firms paying foreign suppliers and investors buying assets abroad. If your currency buys more euros than last year, it has appreciated, or strengthened. If it buys fewer, it has depreciated, or weakened.

cards.headline: What pushes rates around
cards.body: Most big currencies float: their rates are mainly set by the market, through supply and demand. Relatively high interest rates pull in money from abroad, so the currency tends to rise. Relatively high inflation eats away at what a currency buys, so it tends to fall. And expectations feed themselves: if people expect a currency to rise, they buy it, and that can push it up.

mascot.line: Same dollar, same day: good news for your holiday abroad, bad news for exporters.

cards.headline: Strong isn't simply good
cards.body: A stronger dollar helps Americans buying imports or traveling abroad, but a weaker one helps US exporters and foreign tourists visiting the US. Every move has winners and losers. Some countries skip the ride and fix, or peg, their rate against another currency, as the world did under Level 7's Bretton Woods system, when other currencies were fixed to the dollar.

title: From Caravans to Containers
objective: After this level you can trace how trade routes grew from the Silk Road to container ships.
summary: The Silk Road linked China and the West, with goods passed along by middlemen. In 1956, Malcolm McLean's containers made loading ships far cheaper than handling loose cargo.

cards.headline: Silk crossed Asia for centuries, yet almost nobody made the whole trip.
cards.body: On the Silk Road, few people traveled the entire route. Goods moved in stages, handed from middleman to middleman. This level follows how goods traveled, from camel caravans to steel boxes.

cards.headline: The Silk Road
cards.body: The Silk Road was a caravan route of about 6,400 km linking China with the West, carrying goods and ideas between China and Rome. Silk went west; wool, gold and silver went east. Religions traveled it too, and so did diseases. After years as an unsafe, little-used route, it revived under the Mongols. That's when Marco Polo went east, and came home describing Level 5's Chinese paper money.

cards.headline: One sack at a time
cards.body: Ships carried goods much farther than camels, but loading them stayed slow. Sacks, barrels and crates were handled one by one. This loose, break-bulk cargo could take several days to load, so ships often sat in port for long periods. Picture packing for a house move one sock at a time.

cards.fact: April 26, 1956: 58 boxes set sail, and loading got cheap.
cards.context: Trucking entrepreneur Malcolm McLean sent his ship, the Ideal X, from Newark to Houston carrying 58 metal containers. Instead of loose cargo, whole boxes went aboard. Loading a ship the conventional way cost more than $5.80 a ton. Loading McLean's containers cost about 16 cents.

title: Globalization
objective: After this level you can explain how supply chains stretch across many countries.
summary: About half of world trade runs through global supply chains, like the iPhone 3G's. Globalization lowered prices and helped poor countries grow, while job losses piled up in particular places.

cards.headline: In March 2021, one stuck ship held up about $9 billion of trade a day.
cards.body: The Ever Given ran aground in the Suez Canal on March 23 and wasn't refloated until March 29. How could one ship matter so much? Because much of what you buy is pieced together across many countries.

cards.headline: Made in many places
cards.body: About half of global trade now happens inside global supply chains: networks that build products from parts and services sourced around the world. Take the iPhone 3G. Its parts came from firms in Japan, South Korea, Germany and the US. Then it was all assembled in China.

mascot.line: Keep this: the label names where it was finished, not where most of the value was made.

cards.fact: Assembly in China added $6.50 to an iPhone that cost $178.96 to make.
cards.context: That's about 3.6% of the total, by economists Yuqing Xing and Neal Detert's 2010 count. Yet trade statistics recorded all $178.96 as a Chinese export. Remember Level 73's trade balance, exports minus imports? With supply chains, the country on the label isn't always where most of the value was made.

cards.headline: Two sides of the same story
cards.body: Supporters point to prices and growth: globalization lets countries specialize, which lowers prices, and more open economies helped once extremely poor countries grow and cut poverty. Critics point to who paid. Economists David Autor, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson found cheap Chinese imports had cost the US about 2.4 million jobs by 2011, concentrated in places that stayed worse off for years. Meanwhile, consumers nationwide got slightly cheaper goods. Both are true at once.

title: Rich and Poor Countries
objective: After this level you can explain the main reasons some countries are richer than others.
summary: The richest fifth of countries are about 30 times richer than the poorest. Nobel winners link this to institutions; Jeffrey Sachs adds geography and disease; all paths run through productivity.

cards.headline: One town, one fence, two very different lives.
cards.body: Nogales is cut in half by the US–Mexico border fence. People on the Arizona side are generally much better off than their neighbors in Nogales, Sonora. Same town, same weather. So what makes the difference?

cards.fact: The richest 20% of countries are about 30 times richer than the poorest 20%.
cards.context: And the gap is stubborn: the poorest countries have grown richer, but they aren't catching up. Economists offer several explanations, and Nogales is a clue to one of them.

cards.headline: The rules of the game
cards.body: Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson won the 2024 economics Nobel for studying how institutions, a society's rules, affect prosperity. Inclusive institutions, with secure property rights and the rule of law, support long-run growth. Extractive ones benefit a small elite at everyone else's expense. Both halves of Nogales share a climate, ancestors, food and music. So, they argue, the difference is institutions.

cards.headline: Other pieces of the puzzle
cards.body: Not everyone thinks rules explain it all. Economist Jeffrey Sachs argued in 2003 that institutions matter, but not for everything: disease such as malaria and geographic isolation also hold poor countries back. Whichever story you favor, it runs through productivity, the value each worker produces. Productivity rises with education and better technology, and it underpins a country's standard of living.

title: Global Institutions
objective: After this level you can describe what the IMF, the World Bank and the WTO do.
summary: Bretton Woods (1944) created the IMF, which lends in crises with conditions, and the World Bank, which funds development. The WTO (1995) runs trade rules and disputes. Each has critics.

cards.headline: July 1944: the war wasn't over, yet 44 nations planned the postwar economy.
cards.body: Delegates met at the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire. Level 7 showed you the currency system they built. They also created two institutions that still exist: the International Monetary Fund and what is now the World Bank.

cards.headline: The IMF: help, with strings
cards.body: The IMF was set up to watch over exchange rates and lend to countries short of foreign currency to pay their international bills. It still lends in a crisis, with conditions: the borrower agrees to change its economic policies to fix the problems that led it to ask. Critics argue that austere conditions can slow growth, deepen crises and hurt the poorest people.

mascot.line: The IMF and World Bank get mixed up. The IMF lends in a crisis; the Bank funds development.

cards.headline: The World Bank: a builder
cards.body: The Bank's first loan went to France, for rebuilding after the war. When the Marshall Plan took over rebuilding Europe, the Bank turned to power, irrigation and transport projects around the world. Today, part of it gives grants and low-interest loans to help low-income countries invest and develop.

cards.fact: The WTO referees trade among 166 members.
cards.context: The World Trade Organization began on 1 January 1995, succeeding the 1947 General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. It runs trade agreements, hosts negotiations and handles disputes between members, which together account for 98% of world trade. Critics say it favors large corporations and raise concerns about the environment, labor rights and national sovereignty.

title: Checkpoint: Trade and the Global Economy

summary: The Big Mac index tests purchasing power parity with burger prices. One imported washer ties the chapter together: comparative advantage, containers, tariffs, exchange rates, trade balance.

cards.headline: What can a hamburger tell you about a currency?
cards.body: Since 1986, The Economist has compared the price of a Big Mac around the world, as a lighthearted lesson in exchange rates. It's also a good way to pull this chapter together.

cards.headline: The burger test
cards.body: The idea behind it is purchasing power parity: exchange rates should drift toward the rate that makes the same goods cost the same in different countries. If a Big Mac costs less abroad, in dollars, than in the US, that currency may be undervalued; if it costs more, overvalued. Take it with a pinch of salt: one burger can't capture local wages, taxes and other costs of doing business.

cards.headline: One import, the whole chapter
cards.body: Follow an imported washing machine home. Countries specialize where their costs are relatively lowest (Level 72), so it may well be made abroad. Containers made shipping it cheap (Level 76). A tariff can raise its price, as importers pass the cost on (Level 74). A stronger home currency makes imports cheaper; a weaker one, pricier (Level 75). And it arrives as an import, counted in the trade balance (Level 73).

title: What a Company Is
objective: After this level you can explain how companies are owned and organized.
summary: Sole proprietors and partners owe business debts personally. A corporation is a separate legal person with limited liability, as the Salomon case showed. Shareholders elect its board.

cards.headline: A bootmaker's company went bust. Did he have to pay its debts?
cards.body: Aron Salomon made leather boots in London. In 1892 he turned his business into a limited company, and soon afterwards it failed, owing money. The fight over who should pay went all the way to Britain's top court. Its answer still shapes what a company is.

cards.headline: Three ways to own a business
cards.body: The simplest business is a sole proprietorship: one owner, who in law is the business. If it runs up debts, the owner owes them personally, with no limit. A partnership is the same deal shared by two or more owners, and in a general partnership every partner is on the hook. Before 1892, Salomon was a sole proprietor. His boots, and his debts, were all his.

mascot.line: Keep this: a corporation is a separate person in law, so owners can lose only what they put in.

cards.headline: A person made of paperwork
cards.body: A corporation is different. In law it's a separate person: it can own property, sign contracts, and sue or be sued. Its owners have limited liability, so they can lose what they put in, but no more. That was the whole case. Salomon's company failed, and its liquidator argued that Salomon should pay its debts himself. The House of Lords said no: the company was a separate person in law, even though he held nearly all its shares.

cards.headline: Owning isn't running
cards.body: In a corporation, owning and running are split. The owners are shareholders, and they elect a board of directors. The board sets the big goals and policies, then hires officers, like the chief executive officer (CEO), to run the firm day to day. So you can own a slice of a company without ever setting foot in it.

title: Starting a Business
objective: After this level you can explain what an entrepreneur does and what it costs to start a business.
summary: An entrepreneur organizes a business and carries its risk. HP began in a garage with $538. Start-ups face one-time and ongoing costs, and about half last five years.

cards.headline: Two friends, a garage and $538. That's how HP started.
cards.body: Bill Hewlett and Dave Packard began working part-time in a Palo Alto garage. California now honors it as the "Birthplace of Silicon Valley". On day one, though, it was just two people and an idea that might not work.

cards.headline: What an entrepreneur does
cards.body: An entrepreneur is someone who organizes a business, runs it and carries its risk. The word comes from the Old French entreprendre, "to undertake", and that's the job: taking on something that might fail. Hewlett and Packard made it official on January 1, 1939, as a partnership, Level 81's two-owner model. Even the company's name was settled by a coin toss.

cards.headline: What it costs to begin
cards.body: Their $538 of working capital even counted the value of Packard's used drill press. Every start-up has costs. Some are one-time, like equipment, permits and licenses. Others keep coming, like rent, salaries and utilities. The money usually comes from the founders' own savings, from loans, or from investors, who put in cash in return for a share of ownership.

cards.fact: About half of new US businesses are gone within five years.
cards.context: Government statisticians tracked every US business location that opened in March 2013. A year later, 79.6% were still going. After five years, 50.6% were left; after ten, 34.7%. That's the risk hiding inside "undertake". A garage that grows into HP is the famous exception, not the rule.

title: Revenue, Costs and Profit
objective: After this level you can explain how a business makes a profit.
summary: Revenue is price times quantity sold; profit is revenue minus total cost. Fixed costs stay put while variable costs move with output. Amazon lost money in 2002 despite billions in sales.

cards.headline: In 2002, Amazon sold about $3.9 billion of goods. It still lost money.
cards.body: Shoppers were buying and the orders kept coming, yet the year ended in the red. How? Because the money coming in is not the money you get to keep.

mascot.line: Revenue and profit get mixed up. Revenue is what comes in; profit is what's left.

cards.headline: Revenue in, profit left
cards.body: Revenue is what a business takes in from selling: the price of each item times how many it sells. Profit is what's left after paying all the costs: revenue minus total cost. If costs are bigger than revenue, the answer is negative, and that's a loss. Amazon's 2002 revenue was huge, but its costs were bigger still, leaving a loss of about $149 million.

cards.headline: Two kinds of cost
cards.body: Costs come in two kinds. Fixed costs, like the rent on a shop or factory, machinery and advertising, stay the same whether you make one thing or a million. Variable costs, like workers' hours and raw materials, rise and fall with how much you make. Sell more and revenue grows, but variable costs grow right along with it. Only the fixed costs sit still.

cards.fact: In 2003, Amazon finally made a full-year profit: about $35 million.
cards.context: Its net sales that year were about $5.26 billion. So the profit was a sliver of the revenue: less than a penny for every dollar of sales. The lesson: a big revenue number tells you how much a business sells, not how much it keeps.

title: Economies of Scale
objective: After this level you can explain why making more of something can make each one cheaper.
summary: Making more spreads fixed costs over more units, so each costs less: economies of scale. Ford's Model T fell from $850 to $260. Firms that grow too big hit diseconomies of scale.

cards.headline: In 1908, a Model T cost $850. Later it sold for as little as $260.
cards.body: Same basic car, a fraction of the price. The trick wasn't a clearance sale. Ford built more than 15 million of them.

cards.headline: Spreading the fixed costs
cards.body: Remember Level 83's fixed costs? A factory's rent and machinery cost the same whether it turns out ten cars or ten thousand. Divide total cost by the number made and you get the average cost of each one. Make more, and the fixed costs are spread thinner, so each unit's share shrinks. It's like splitting a delivery fee: the more friends sharing it, the less each one pays.

cards.headline: Economies of scale
cards.body: When making more lowers the cost of each unit, economists call it economies of scale. Ford rode them hard. Mass production let it sell the Model T cheaply, and from 1908 to 1927 the price fell from $850 to as little as $260. By the early 1920s, more than half of the registered cars in the world were Fords.

cards.fact: Bigger isn't always cheaper.
cards.context: A firm can grow so large that it's hard to manage. Layers of managers try to talk to workers and to each other, messages get garbled, and work and materials stop flowing smoothly. Then the cost of each unit starts climbing again. Economists call that diseconomies of scale.

title: Division of Labor
objective: After this level you can explain Adam Smith's pin factory and why specializing raises output.
summary: In Adam Smith's pin factory (1776), ten workers splitting about 18 operations made upwards of 48,000 pins a day. Specializing builds skill, saves time and leads to machines.

cards.headline: One worker alone: perhaps not one pin a day. Ten together: 48,000.
cards.body: That's Adam Smith's famous pin factory, from the first chapter of The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776. Same people, same wire. The difference was how they split up the work.

cards.headline: Eighteen small jobs
cards.body: Smith counted about 18 distinct operations in making a pin. One worker draws out the wire, another straightens it, a third cuts it, and so on down the line. Ten workers, each sticking to a few steps, could make upwards of 48,000 pins a day: about 4,800 each. Working alone, Smith reckoned, each could certainly not make 20, and perhaps not even one.

cards.headline: Why specializing works
cards.body: Smith gave three reasons. Practice: doing one task over and over makes you better at it. Time: nobody loses minutes switching from one kind of work to the next. Machines: dividing the work leads to machines that save labor. Same hands, far more pins.

cards.fact: Smith also saw the dark side of dividing labor.
cards.context: Later in the same book, he warned that a worker who spends a whole life on a few simple operations "generally becomes as stupid and ignorant as it is possible for a human creature to become." Harsh words from the man who made the pin factory famous. Specializing multiplies output; it doesn't promise interesting work.

title: What Sets Wages
objective: After this level you can explain what determines how much a job pays.
summary: A wage is the price of labor. Productive, well-trained workers are in more demand and in shorter supply. Dirty or dangerous jobs pay extra: a compensating differential.

cards.headline: In Adam Smith's day, a coal miner could out-earn a skilled blacksmith.
cards.body: The blacksmith had the craft. The miner had the dirt, the danger and the dark. So what really sets how much a job pays?

cards.headline: A wage is a price
cards.body: A wage is the price of labor. In the labor market, employers are the buyers, demanding workers, and workers are the sellers, supplying their time. Employers want more workers when those workers produce more, for example because they're better trained, or when customers want more of what they make. On the other side, jobs that need more education or training have fewer people able to do them.

cards.fact: In 2024, US workers with a bachelor's degree earned a median $1,543 a week.
cards.context: That compares with $930 for those with only a high school diploma, counting full-time workers aged 25 and over. Both sides of the market are at work: training can make workers more productive, which raises demand for them, and fewer people have it, which limits supply.

cards.headline: Paying for the dirt
cards.body: Back to the coal miner. Smith noticed that wages vary with the ease or hardship, and the cleanliness or dirtiness, of the work. A journeyman blacksmith seldom earned in 12 hours what a coal miner earned in 8, because mining was dirtier, more dangerous and done underground. Economists call this extra pay a compensating differential: to fill an unpleasant job, employers have to make it worth someone's while.

title: Unions
objective: After this level you can explain what unions are and how collective bargaining works.
summary: A union is workers acting together. It bargains collectively over wages, hours and conditions, and can strike. The 1936 to 1937 Flint sit-down strike won recognition of the UAW.

cards.headline: In 1936, autoworkers in Flint went on strike without leaving work.
cards.body: They sat down inside General Motors' plants and stayed put, for 44 days. Why would a strike work better from the inside?

cards.headline: Bargaining as a team
cards.body: One worker asking for a raise is easy to turn down. A union is an association of workers who act together to improve their conditions. Through collective bargaining, the union's representatives negotiate with the employer over wages, hours and working conditions. If talks fail, workers can strike: a collective refusal to work on the employer's terms.

cards.headline: Why sit down?
cards.body: Strikers who walk out can be replaced by other workers. So from December 30, 1936, the Flint strikers occupied GM's plants instead of picketing outside, which kept them out of the weather and hard to replace. On February 11, 1937, General Motors agreed to recognize their union, the United Auto Workers. Sit-down strikes like theirs are now counted among illegal kinds of strike.

cards.fact: About 1 in 10 US workers belongs to a union.
cards.context: In 2025, 10.0% of US wage and salary workers were union members, about half the 20.1% of 1983. Where a union does bargain, Level 86's price of labor isn't settled one worker at a time: it's negotiated for the group.

title: Automation and Jobs
objective: After this level you can explain how machines have changed work, from looms to robots.
summary: Luddites smashed machines from 1811. Farm work fell from 41% of US jobs in 1900 to 1.9% in 2000, and ATMs changed tellers' work. Machines take over tasks; work shifts.

cards.headline: In 1811, English workers started smashing machines.
cards.body: They signed threatening letters in the name of "Ned Ludd", a leader who never existed. What were they really fighting?

cards.headline: Not against machines
cards.body: The Luddite attacks began near Nottingham in March 1811, on knitting machines called stocking frames. But the Luddites weren't against machines as such. They objected to owners using them to get around labor standards, turning out cheaper, lower-quality work. Parliament's answer was harsh: breaking a machine became a capital crime.

cards.headline: Where did the farmers go?
cards.body: The biggest shift came on farms. In 1900, 41% of American workers worked in agriculture; by 2000, just 1.9% did. Tractors replaced horses and mules, and more productive farms freed a huge share of the population for jobs outside farming. The farm jobs went. The workers moved on.

mascot.line: Keep this: machines take over tasks, and the jobs change around them.

cards.headline: Machines take tasks
cards.body: ATMs were supposed to finish off bank tellers. Instead, each urban branch needed fewer of them: 13 instead of 20 between 1988 and 2004. But banks opened 43% more urban branches, so teller jobs didn't disappear. They changed, from counting cash toward helping customers with other services.

cards.fact: The first industrial robot clocked in at General Motors in 1961.
cards.context: Unimate, a robot arm, lifted and stacked hot die-cast metal parts. It's Level 85's third reason in steel: divide work into simple steps, and machines that save labor follow.

title: Advertising
objective: After this level you can explain how advertising shapes what people buy.
summary: Advertising can inform (eyeglasses cost more where ads were banned) and persuade (brand loyalty, "A Diamond Is Forever"). Pigou argued rival ads may simply cancel out.

cards.headline: Four words from 1947: "A Diamond Is Forever."
cards.body: Copywriter Frances Gerety wrote them for De Beers. In 1999, Advertising Age named them the best advertising slogan of the 20th century. How can a few words change what people buy?

cards.headline: Ads that inform
cards.body: Some ads are simply news: this exists, here's what it does, here's the price. That helps you compare. In 1972, economist Lee Benham found that eyeglasses cost more in US states that banned advertising than in states that allowed it. When shoppers can't see prices, they can't easily compare them.

cards.headline: Ads that persuade
cards.body: Other ads work on feelings. Blindfolded, many people can't tell common ketchups apart, yet habit and advertising give them strong favorites. De Beers's four words helped make the diamond solitaire the standard engagement ring. Before, engagement rings often used colored gems, small diamonds or even pearls. The stone didn't change. The story around it did.

cards.fact: Rival ads can cancel each other out.
cards.context: In 1920, economist A. C. Pigou pointed out that when two competing firms each spend to lure customers from the other, the spending may simply neutralize itself, leaving both where they'd be if neither had advertised. Picture two neighbors in a shouting match: both get louder, and nobody hears anything new.

title: Checkpoint: Companies and Work
objective: After this level you can explain how businesses make profits, set wages and change with technology.
summary: Coase (1937): firms exist because markets have transaction costs, so managers direct work inside. From pin factories to robots, companies turn costs into revenue and pay wages for labor.

cards.headline: If markets work so well, why do companies exist at all?
cards.body: In theory, you could hire a stranger for every single task, one deal at a time. In 1937, economist Ronald Coase asked why businesses don't simply do that.

cards.headline: The cost of using the market
cards.body: Coase's answer: markets aren't free to use. Every deal means finding out prices and negotiating a separate contract, costs now called transaction costs. A firm cuts them. Instead of a fresh contract for each task, managers direct the work inside. The idea helped earn Coase the 1991 Nobel Prize in economics, and it explains why this chapter's companies exist at all.

cards.headline: The chapter through Coase's eyes
cards.body: Look back through Coase's lens. A corporation is a legal person that can own property and sign contracts. An entrepreneur organizes it and carries the risk. Inside, work is directed rather than bargained task by task. Profit is revenue minus total cost, and economies of scale push the cost of each unit down. Wages are the price of the labor it hires.

title: Adam Smith and the Invisible Hand
objective: After this level you can explain Smith's idea that self-interest can serve the common good through markets.
summary: Adam Smith argued in 1776 that self-interested trade can serve everyone, as if led by an invisible hand. He also gave government duties and distrusted collusion, and critics say the hand often fails.

cards.headline: Your dinner doesn't depend on the butcher's kindness. Adam Smith said so.
cards.body: In 1776, the Scottish philosopher published The Wealth of Nations. One idea in it became among the most quoted, and most argued over, in all of economics.

cards.headline: The butcher, the brewer and the baker
cards.body: Smith's point was down to earth. You don't get dinner because the butcher, the brewer or the baker feels generous toward you. You get it because selling to you serves their own interest. Nobody has to love you for the bread to show up. Each baker minds his own business, and the town gets fed anyway.

cards.fact: Smith used the phrase 'invisible hand' just once in The Wealth of Nations.
cards.context: In it, a person who "intends only his own gain" is "led by an invisible hand to promote an end which was no part of his intention." The idea: good outcomes for everyone can grow out of many self-interested choices, with no one arranging them. Later writers stretched it, more controversially, into a claim that free markets always deliver the best possible result.

cards.headline: Smith's fine print
cards.body: Smith was no enemy of government. He gave it three duties: defense, justice, and public works like roads and bridges that help society but wouldn't pay a private builder. And he didn't trust business to police itself. People of the same trade, he warned, seldom meet without the talk ending in a conspiracy against the public, or some scheme to raise prices.

cards.headline: The critics
cards.body: Modern critics push further. In 2002, economist Joseph Stiglitz wrote that the invisible hand is invisible, at least in part, because it isn't there. So the question Smith raised stays open: how much good can self-interest do on its own, and where does it need help?

title: Karl Marx and Capitalism's Critics
objective: After this level you can explain Marx's critique of capitalism and how far it spread.
summary: Marx argued owners keep the value workers create as profit and predicted workers would overthrow capitalism. Communism once ruled a third of the world; critics rejected his theory of value.

cards.headline: Smith saw a town fed by self-interest. Marx saw workers being shortchanged.
cards.body: In 1848, Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published The Communist Manifesto. In 1867 came the first volume of Das Kapital. Marx's question: who really creates the value in what a factory makes, and who keeps it?

mascot.line: Notice the link: Marx built on Smith, Level 91's thinker, and reached a very different view.

cards.headline: Where does profit come from?
cards.body: Marx built on concepts inherited from Adam Smith and David Ricardo, including the labor theory of value: a product's value is set by the labor it takes to make it. Follow that through and profit looks suspicious. If workers create the value, but owners pay them just enough to live on and keep the rest, that leftover is what Marx called surplus value. To him, profit rested on exploitation.

cards.headline: A prediction of revolution
cards.body: Marx saw history as a series of class struggles, and under capitalism that meant owners of capital against workers. He expected wealth to pile up in fewer hands, and he and Engels predicted the industrial working class would one day overthrow capitalism. He pictured that revolution in industrialized countries. The revolution that did come was in mostly agrarian Russia, under Lenin's version of his ideas.

cards.fact: For much of the 20th century, about a third of the world lived under communist governments.
cards.context: Leaders including Lenin and Mao built on Marx's writings to impose communism on more than twenty countries, and his ideas inspired labor and socialist movements in western Europe. Critics went after the foundation. The Austrian school argued that a thing's value comes from its ability to satisfy wants, not the labor used to make it, and labor itself varies so much in skill that value is hard to measure that way.

title: Keynes and Spending in a Slump
objective: After this level you can explain Keynes's argument for government spending during a slump.
summary: Keynes argued unemployment comes from too little spending, so in a slump government should spend, even by borrowing. From the 1970s, monetarists led by Milton Friedman gained ground.

cards.headline: An economist once suggested burying banknotes in old coal mines.
cards.body: That was John Maynard Keynes, in his 1936 book The General Theory. It sounds like a joke. It was a serious answer to a serious question: what should happen when an economy stops spending?

cards.headline: Nobody buys, nobody hires
cards.body: Keynes's big idea was total spending in the economy, which economists call aggregate demand. Businesses won't hire workers to make goods that can't be sold. So when spending falls, jobs go with it. In Keynes's view, the root of unemployment was too little demand, and cutting wages wouldn't cure it. Something had to get people spending again.

cards.headline: Government steps in
cards.body: His fix: if households and businesses won't spend, government can, even if it has to borrow and run a budget deficit. Hence the coal mines. Bury banknotes in bottles, let firms dig them up, and the digging alone would put people to work. Then Keynes added the sensible part: "It would, indeed, be more sensible to build houses." Useful spending beats useless spending, but in a slump, both beat none.

cards.fact: Keynes helped design Level 7's Bretton Woods system.
cards.context: At the 1944 conference, he was one of the architects of the postwar system of fixed exchange rates. His ideas guided most Western governments until the 1970s, when monetarism eclipsed them. Its leader was Milton Friedman, Level 6's Yap storyteller, who argued government should steady the economy only by growing the money supply at a steady rate. And Friedrich Hayek, who debated Keynes in the 1930s, never accepted that Keynes had won.

title: Markets, Plans and Mixed Economies
objective: After this level you can compare market, planned and mixed economies.
summary: Markets spread decisions among buyers and sellers; command economies take goals from rulers. Hayek argued prices carry knowledge no planner can gather. Most real economies are mixed.

cards.headline: Tin gets scarce. Thousands of people use less of it. Nobody gave an order.
cards.body: Economist Friedrich Hayek posed that puzzle in 1945. Every economy has to decide what gets made. The real fight is over who decides: a planner, the market, or a bit of both.

items.label: Market economy
points: Decisions spread out among buyers and sellers

mascot.line: You met Hayek's tin in Level 50. Here it becomes an argument about who decides.

cards.headline: Prices as messages
cards.body: Hayek's argument: the knowledge an economy runs on exists in no single mind. It's scattered, with each person knowing things about their own resources that no planner ever can. Prices gather it up. When tin gets scarce, users don't need to know why. The price rises, and they use less. Hayek compared the price system to a kind of telecommunications system.

cards.fact: The inefficiency of communist economies helped bring down the Soviet Union in 1991.
cards.context: Soviet planners at Gosplan turned the party's goals into national plans. Hayek had argued no planner could gather knowledge scattered across a whole society. But markets don't run on prices alone either. Even market economies rely on government to protect property, enforce contracts, prevent fraud and collect taxes. That's why most real economies are mixed: part market, part government.

title: Behavioral Economics
objective: After this level you can explain why real people don't always act rationally with money.
summary: Behavioral economics tests whether people are perfectly rational. Loss aversion makes owners value things more, and mental accounting sorts money into jars. Experience may shrink these effects.

cards.headline: Hand someone a mug and it instantly becomes worth more. To them.
cards.body: In a 1990 experiment, economists gave mugs to randomly chosen people and let them sell to people who didn't get one. Theory said about half the mugs should change hands. Far fewer did.

cards.headline: Rational on paper
cards.body: Traditional economic theory assumes people have good information and process it perfectly. Behavioral economics checks that against how people really behave. One of its founders wasn't even an economist: psychologist Daniel Kahneman, whose work with Amos Tversky produced "Prospect Theory" in 1979. He won the 2002 economics Nobel for bringing psychological research into economics.

cards.headline: Losses hurt more
cards.body: So why did the mug owners hang on? Richard Thaler's answer is loss aversion: losing something feels worse than gaining the same thing feels good. Once the mug is yours, selling it feels like a loss. That's the endowment effect: we value things more simply because we own them. Anyone who has tried to clear out a closet knows the feeling.

cards.headline: Money in labeled jars
cards.body: Thaler also described mental accounting: we sort money into separate accounts in our heads and judge each decision on its own. Losing money even hurts less if you're still "in the black" in that mental account, which Thaler calls the house money effect. That work helped win him the 2017 economics Nobel for his contributions to behavioral economics.

cards.fact: Experience may shrink the mug effect.
cards.context: Not everyone thinks these quirks run the world. In 2003, economist John List studied real marketplaces and found that as traders gained market experience, the endowment effect faded. A real quirk, then, but maybe not a permanent one.

title: Game Theory
objective: After this level you can explain the prisoner's dilemma and why cooperation is hard.
summary: In the prisoner's dilemma, each player does better by betraying whatever the other does, yet both end up worse off. When the game repeats with no known end, cooperation can pay, as tit for tat showed.

cards.headline: Two shops cut prices to steal each other's customers. Both end up poorer.
cards.body: Neither gains a single customer, and both earn smaller profits. Why would two sensible owners do that? Game theory has a famous answer, and it starts in a police station.

mascot.line: Keep this: each player's best move, taken by both, leaves both worse off.

cards.headline: The prisoner's dilemma
cards.body: Two suspects are questioned in separate rooms. If both stay silent, each gets a year. If both confess, five years each. If one confesses and the other stays silent, the confessor walks free and the silent one gets 20 years. Work it through: whatever your partner does, confessing leaves you better off. So both confess, and both serve five years instead of one.
cards.callout: Both silent: 1 year each · Both confess: 5 years each

cards.fact: The prisoner's dilemma was invented before it had any prisoners.
cards.context: Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher devised the game at the RAND Corporation in 1950. Albert Tucker added the prison story later, to make it easier to explain. The same trap turns up far from any jail: in an arms race, two nations keep buying weapons, neither gains an advantage, and both end up poorer. The price-cutting shops are in it too.

cards.headline: Play again, and trust can pay
cards.body: There's a way out: meet again. When the game repeats and nobody knows which round is last, cooperation can emerge. In Robert Axelrod's computer tournaments, Anatol Rapoport's tit for tat did famously well: cooperate first, then copy your partner's last move. Axelrod found that every "nice" strategy, one that never betrays first, beat every strategy that wasn't.

title: Inequality
objective: After this level you can explain how income and wealth inequality are measured.
summary: The Gini coefficient runs from 0 (everyone has the same) to 1 (one person has it all). Wealth is far more unequal than income: in OECD countries, the top 10% hold about half of wealth.

cards.headline: Ten friends split a pizza. How do you put one number on how fairly?
cards.body: Everyone gets a slice: that's one extreme. One friend eats the whole thing: that's the other. Economists measure how evenly a country shares its income on exactly that kind of scale.

cards.headline: The Gini coefficient
cards.body: Italian statistician Corrado Gini devised it in 1912. A Gini of 0 means perfect equality: everyone has the same income. A Gini of 1 means one person gets all of it and everyone else gets nothing. It's tied to the Lorenz curve, a chart from 1905 that plots what share of income goes to what share of the people.

mascot.line: Income and wealth get mixed up. Income flows in; wealth is what you own.

cards.headline: Income isn't wealth
cards.body: Income is a flow: the money coming in. Wealth is a stock: what you own. And wealth is shared far less evenly. Across 28 OECD countries, the richest 10% of households held 52% of all household wealth, while the top 10% of earners got 24% of income. On average, wealth inequality ran about twice as high as income inequality.

cards.fact: Two very different countries can have the same Gini.
cards.context: The Gini shows how unequal a distribution is, but not why. Two countries with very different income patterns can land on the same score. And some countries measure consumption rather than income, which can miss how much wealth the richest households hold. One number is a starting point, not the whole story.

title: Externalities
objective: After this level you can explain costs like pollution that fall on people outside a deal.
summary: An externality is the effect of a deal on someone outside it, like pollution. Pigou proposed taxing such costs; Coase argued that when deals are cheap to make, people can bargain their way to a fix.

cards.headline: An outdoor concert sells tickets. The neighbors hear every song.
cards.body: They never bought a ticket and never agreed to the noise, but the deal between the band and the fans lands on them anyway. Economists have a name for that.

cards.headline: Costs that leak out
cards.body: An externality is the effect of a deal on a third party who is outside it. Pollution is the classic negative one: a factory's costs cover its workers and materials, but not the harm its smoke does to the neighbors. Because nobody pays for that harm, the market makes too much of the product. Externalities can be good, too: research that others build on is a standard example.

cards.headline: Pigou: send the bill
cards.body: In The Economics of Welfare, published in 1920, economist Arthur Pigou proposed a fix. Tax activities that impose costs on others; subsidize ones that spread benefits. The tax puts the missing cost back into the price. A carbon tax is the modern example, ideally set equal to the social cost of carbon.

mascot.line: Pigou says tax it; Coase says bargain. Both are asking who pays for the harm.

cards.fact: Ronald Coase asked: why not let the neighbors bargain?
cards.context: In his 1960 paper "The Problem of Social Cost", Coase challenged Pigou's approach. Picture a rancher whose cattle trample a farmer's crops. The farmer could simply pay the rancher to keep fewer cattle. If making a deal costs little, the two can bargain to an efficient fix without government, whoever the law favors. The catch: deal-making costs range from negligible to enormous. Coase won the 1991 economics Nobel.

title: The Economics of Your Life
objective: After this level you can apply the tree's big ideas to everyday choices about work, saving and spending.
summary: Keynes's 15-hour week never came, but longer retirements added leisure. Defaults shape how people save, and the sunk cost effect shows spent money steering choices.

cards.headline: Big ideas, small choices: your job, your savings, tonight's ticket.
cards.body: Economics isn't only about nations and markets. Its ideas show up in how much you work, whether you save, and whether you sit through a play you're not enjoying.

cards.headline: Work: Keynes's 15-hour week
cards.body: In 1930, Keynes predicted that a century later, living standards would be four to eight times higher and people might work just 15 hours a week. Economist Nicholas Crafts concluded the short week won't arrive by 2030. But the free time turned up somewhere else: in the UK, expected lifetime hours of leisure and home production rose 58% between 1931 and 2011, reflecting longer lives and longer retirements.

cards.headline: Saving: the power of the default
cards.body: Behavioral economists find that small details shape big decisions. One is the default: what happens unless you actively choose something else. Another is timing. Promising to save more in the future, especially after a raise, feels easier than saving more today, and Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi built their Save More Tomorrow plan on that. Critics call such nudges paternalistic; supporters stress that joining is voluntary and you can opt out any time.

cards.fact: Paying full price made people go to more plays.
cards.context: In a 1985 study, Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer sold theater season tickets at full price or at random discounts. Over the next six months, the full-price buyers went to more plays, though the money was spent either way. That's the sunk cost effect: a greater tendency to keep going with something once money, effort or time has gone into it.
